standards.statement: Analyze AI systems to differentiate the types of problems they address.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should explore and compare different types of AI systems to understand how they work and what problems they solve. They should analyze generative AI (e.g., chatbots or image creators) and discriminative AI (e.g., image classifiers) to examine how each supports real-world applications (e.g., language translation, image recognition, sentiment analysis, recommendations, game playing).
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to evaluate the performance or quality of AI systems. Students are not expected to train, build, or modify AI models.

implementation_examples.description: After examining a workforce sector (e.g., healthcare), students identify a challenge (e.g., detecting medical conditions from images or predicting patient outcomes) and analyze how different AI systems (e.g., discriminative systems such as image recognition tools vs. generative systems such as medical chatbots) can address these problems. They compare systems that classify data, generate content, or make predictions and analyze how each type of system corresponds to a different class of problem.

Students act as AI product consultants for an arts organization and analyze several AI tools designed to support creative work. They distinguish between systems that classify artworks (e.g., identifying artistic styles), generate new content (e.g., producing images or music based on prompts), or make predictions (e.g., forecasting trends in art preferences). Students then outline how each type of AI system correlates to a different kind of problem the organization is trying to address.

standards.statement: Modify AI system training data to improve fairness and accuracy in outputs.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should mitigate bias and improve accuracy by modifying the data used to train an AI model. They should investigate changes in accuracy by modifying training data, making simple changes like improving data representation or balance, and keeping the changes that lead to better results. For example, students could analyze a facial-recognition model's poor performance on certain groups of users, identify the lack of diversity in the training dataset as a source of bias, and add additional examples representing the underrepresented groups to improve system performance.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to understand the mathematical formulas behind fairness metrics or analyze why different fairness measures cannot be satisfied at the same time.

practices.practice: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.

implementation_examples.description: Students are given a pre-trained machine learning model that was trained on a dataset known to have a specific demographic bias. They use test data from an underrepresented group to quantify the bias within the model. They then investigate the training data to identify the source of the bias, likely an unbalanced or poorly representative dataset. Students modify the training data to improve representation and observe how the changes lead to a measurable increase in accuracy and a decrease in bias for the targeted demographic.

Students apply an AI hiring assistant trained on historical resume data (e.g., a set of resumes from a company's top-performing employees) to some input and discover that some applicants are ranked lower due to patterns in the dataset used to train the model. They investigate how the composition of the training data (e.g., overrepresentation of certain school affiliations or extracurricular activities) influences the model's decisions and modify the training dataset to improve balance and reduce bias in the system's recommendations.

standards.statement: Create an application using pre-existing supervised learning models to make predictions or classifications.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should create a functional application (e.g., to classify, to predict) by selecting and integrating an appropriate, pre-existing supervised learning model. For example, students could use a pretrained image classification model (e.g., from a library) and integrate it into a simple web or mobile application that allows users to upload a photo and receive a prediction of the object in the image.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to train models from scratch using raw data, develop production-ready applications, or work with advanced architectures requiring specialized hardware (e.g., large language models, deep convolutional networks with dozens of layers).

implementation_examples.description: Students build a Lunchroom Food-Rescue Predictor by integrating a pre-existing supervised classification model into an application that predicts whether a cafeteria food item will be left over based on factors such as the day, the menu type, and school events.

Students build a tool that reads a movie review and predicts whether the sentiment is positive or negative by integrating a pre-trained sentiment analysis model. Students test the tool with new reviews and evaluate the accuracy of its predictions.

standards.statement: Compare data representations and how representation choice constrains applicable algorithms.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should analyze the trade-offs between different data representations (e.g., tabular vs. relational data, graph vs. network data, image vs. pixel data, text vs. sequence data) and articulate how the chosen representation dictates the suitable class of algorithms for analysis.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to develop custom data representations, convert data into multiple representations, or mathematically prove why certain algorithms cannot work with specific data representations. Students are not required to work with specialized data formats beyond common types (e.g., tabular, graph, image, text).

implementation_examples.description: Students perform a comparative analysis using two different computational tasks. First, for a social network problem (e.g., finding all mutual friends), students compare representing the network as a tabular format (e.g., a list of [Person A, Person B] pairs) and then as a graph data structure. Then for a simple search algorithm, they articulate how the algorithm (like iterating through a table) is feasible but inefficient, whereas a specialized graph traversal algorithm (like breadth-first search, depth-first search) is necessary and most efficient to find paths and connections within the graph representation, demonstrating the constraint imposed by the representation.

Students examine a dataset describing transportation routes that can be represented in multiple ways (e.g., a table listing connections and distances between locations, a network diagram showing routes between cities, a grid representing travel times across a map). They analyze how different representations support different types of analysis and algorithms (e.g., searching a table for route information, identifying connected routes in a network, analyzing patterns in map-based travel data). Students then articulate how the choice of data representation influences the computational methods that can be applied (e.g., table searches to find route information, network traversal methods to identify connected routes).

standards.statement: Evaluate when AI versus non-AI computational solutions are appropriate for real-world problems.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should evaluate a real-world problem and systematically critique the trade-offs, feasibility, and appropriateness of AI-based solutions versus non-AI computational solutions. For example, students could evaluate whether to use a pre-trained image classification model (AI) to identify defective parts using assembly line photos or use a traditional image-processing algorithm that checks for specific pixel color ranges or geometric shapes (non-AI). Students should assess factors like data availability and interpretability, computational resources, and accuracy needed.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to implement AI or non-AI solutions for real-world problems. Students are not expected to produce detailed cost estimates, but recognizing that cost is a factor in choosing between approaches is appropriate.

implementation_examples.description: Students are presented with a problem (e.g., that of a small, local library needing a system to manage and recommend books). Students define the problem, including the required accuracy and computing resources. Then students propose two distinct computational solutions, one that uses a deterministic algorithmic approach and one that uses an AI-based approach. Students evaluate both solutions based on criteria such as complexity, explainability, accuracy, and/or adaptability. Lastly, students prepare a short report or presentation recommending one solution to the library, justifying their choice based on the complete analysis, focusing on the trade-offs between the two approaches.

Students analyze a real-world consumer problem (e.g., a grocery store deciding how to reduce food waste) and compare an AI-based solution with a non-AI computational approach. Students define the problem constraints, including data availability, required accuracy, and ease of explanation to store managers. They then propose two solutions: a non-AI approach using simple rules or historical averages to predict demand and an AI-based approach using a machine learning model trained on past sales, weather, and seasonal data. Students evaluate the trade-offs between the two approaches in terms of complexity, interpretability, resource requirements, adaptability, and potential impact and recommend one solution with a clear justification grounded in practical considerations.

standards.statement: Examine how data flows through a neural network structure.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should examine how input data moves through a neural network's layers, how weights and activation functions modify the data at each step, and how the final output is generated. They should conceptually trace how a numerical input value flows through a single neuron, is modified by the weight and bias, and is then transformed by the activation function before moving to the next layer. Students should explain this process clearly, using appropriate vocabulary and visual representations (e.g., diagrams, annotated examples).
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to implement neural networks from scratch, understand the mathematical formulas for backpropagation, or work with advanced architectures (recurrent neural networks, transformers, convolutional neural networks with many layers).

implementation_examples.description: Students trace how a number moves through a simple neural network. Given a numerical input, a weight, a bias, and an activation function, students calculate how the input is multiplied by the weight, adjusted by the bias, and transformed by the activation function in a single neuron. They then articulate, using words and a simple diagram, how the neuron's output becomes the input to the next layer and how the network produces a final output. The focus is on clearly articulating each step in how data flows through the network, not on coding or using simulation tools.

Students examine how a neural network processes images by tracing how a handwritten digit moves through the network. The image is represented as numerical pixel values that pass through layers of neurons, where each layer transforms the data using weights, biases, and activation functions. Students then articulate how these transformations enable the network to produce a final prediction for which digit the image represents.

standards.statement: Apply data acquisition, cleaning, and transformation techniques to prepare data for AI analysis.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should perform hands-on application of data preparation steps, including acquiring data from sources (e.g., comma-separated values [CSV] files, public APIs, web scraping of small-scale data), identifying and handling missing values (imputation or removal), and performing basic transformations (normalization) necessary for training an AI model. For example, students could use a programming library to load a raw dataset, clean inconsistent entries, convert non-numeric features into a machine-readable format, and split the data into training and testing sets before model application.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to work with datasets requiring distributed computing infrastructure or implement advanced data preprocessing algorithms from scratch.

implementation_examples.description: Students are given a real-world, messy dataset containing common issues such as inconsistent spelling, missing entries, and text-based categorical features. They use a data manipulation library to: (a) identify data quality issues through descriptive statistics and visualization, (b) clean the data by handling outliers and inputting or dropping missing values, and (c) standardize/normalize numeric features to ensure all inputs are appropriately scaled for model training. The final output is a clean, processed data file ready for an AI classification or regression task.

Students investigate a publicly available dataset related to air quality, housing prices, or student performance for missing values, inconsistent formatting, and categorical text fields. They apply cleaning and transformation techniques (e.g., imputing missing data, encoding categorical features, normalizing numerical values). They then normalize selected numerical features and split the data into training and testing sets.

standards.statement: Plan safeguards for AI systems that protect human well-being and privacy while ensuring meaningful human involvement in decision-making.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should plan safeguards in AI systems focusing on practical measures to protect privacy, ensure human well-being, and maintain meaningful human involvement in critical decision-making processes. For example, students could analyze a scenario where an AI is used for medical diagnosis and formulate a human-in-the-loop workflow where the AI provides a recommendation, but a qualified human doctor is required to make the final, auditable diagnosis, thereby ensuring meaningful human involvement and protecting patient well-being.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to develop formal methods for verifying AI safety.

implementation_examples.description: Students analyze a proposed multi-agent traffic management system in which autonomous traffic lights communicate to optimize traffic flow. They identify potential risks related to privacy, system failures, or excessive automation and plan safeguards (e.g., manual override controls, data minimization practices, human monitoring dashboards). Students then hypothesize how these safeguards help protect public safety, privacy, and human oversight in the system.

Students examine an AI-enabled system used in a sensitive context (e.g., hiring screening, school discipline monitoring, healthcare scheduling). They identify risks related to fairness, privacy, or over-automation and plan safeguards (e.g., human-in-the-loop review processes, clear override mechanisms, limits on data collection). Students then hypothesize how these safeguards ensure that humans remain responsible for critical decisions influenced by AI systems.

standards.statement: Analyze the potential biases and limitations of AI systems.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should employ both qualitative and quantitative methods to identify and analyze systemic issues in AI systems, investigating how social, cultural, and historical biases are encoded in the training data, model architecture, and application design. Students should analyze AI systems they created themselves as well as AI systems created by others. For example, students could perform a comparison of a facial recognition model created by others versus a text classifier created by the student, using metrics to show how performance varies across different demographic groups and articulating how those performance gaps may be influenced by specific training data limitations.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to develop novel bias detection algorithms, perform complex causal inference to determine the root cause of systemic inequality, or access proprietary, nonpublic model weights and data from systems created by industry.

12. Design computing technologies that empower and inform users.

implementation_examples.description: Students are given a dataset and a basic pre-trained AI model. They use techniques like slicing the data to analyze the model's performance on a specific, potentially marginalized sub-population (e.g., non-native English speakers, a specific geographic region). They then write a Critical Analysis Report that (1) quantifies the performance gap using an appropriate fairness metric, (2) qualitatively hypothesizes the source of the bias (e.g., underrepresentation in the training data, historical bias in the labels), and (3) details the limitations of the system if deployed in an uncontrolled real-world scenario, focusing on the potential for social harm.

Students conduct a bias audit of AI systems used in different contexts, such as resume screening or sentiment analysis of customer feedback. They compare model performance across different groups (e.g., language background, writing style, geographic region) and investigate how factors such as training data composition, labeling practices, or design assumptions may encode social, cultural, or historical biases. Students then summarize their findings in a report explaining the sources of bias and the potential risks of deploying these systems at scale.

standards.statement: Analyze the environmental impacts of widespread AI adoption.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should quantitatively and qualitatively analyze the environmental impacts of AI, specifically focusing on the energy consumption required for model training and inference and the resulting carbon footprint and electronic waste. Students should consider how these environmental impacts affect different communities, recognizing that the costs of AI infrastructure (e.g., data center energy use, water consumption, e-waste disposal) are often concentrated in specific regions and populations. For example, students could compare the estimated carbon dioxide emissions generated by training a large language model versus the energy used by a local, optimized model running on an edge device.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to conduct complex, full life-cycle assessments for computing hardware.

implementation_examples.description: Students analyze the environmental impacts of AI-supporting infrastructure such as data centers. They assess factors such as energy consumption, water usage for cooling, and demands on local electrical grids and examine how these impacts affect surrounding communities. Students then compare and contrast how design choices, efficiency improvements, or deployment strategies could reduce the environmental impact of widespread AI adoption.

Students analyze the environmental impacts of large-scale AI systems (e.g., recommendation engines, generative AI services). Using publicly available information, they examine how energy consumption, data center operations, and model training contribute to carbon emissions and resource use. Students then articulate how design choices, efficiency improvements, or deployment strategies could reduce the environmental impact of widespread AI adoption.

standards.statement: Integrate a prebuilt AI agent into an application.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should integrate a prebuilt AI agent into a computational application to accomplish a specific task, given information on available AI agents or services. Such prebuilt AI agent templates may include web search, data analysis, creative writing, or customer support bots.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to design or train their own agent.

implementation_examples.description: Students integrate a prebuilt AI agent into a simple application, such as a chatbot that helps answer frequently asked questions for assignments. Given information on a set of AI agents, students select one appropriate for their task and connect it to their application's input and output. The students then examine the agent's autonomous search accuracy using questions such as "When is the next lab report due?" "What are the requirements for the term paper?"

Students integrate a prebuilt AI agent into a digital tool that assists with moderating online discussions in a classroom forum. They examine how well the agent identifies inappropriate content or flags messages for review. Students then analyze how integrating the AI agent improves or limits the functionality of the application.

standards.statement: Analyze how AI tools shape user experiences for people with diverse backgrounds and characteristics.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should analyze how AI tools produce different user experiences across diverse characteristics and backgrounds (e.g., socioeconomic status, cultural background, geographic region, language). They should examine differences in outputs and interactions and explain how training data, system design, or deployment context contribute to those differences. For example, students could analyze how a voice assistant performs for speakers with different accents or how a recommendation algorithm exposes users to different content based on demographic characteristics.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to design user experience studies for AI tools or implement adaptive personalization systems.

practices.practice: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.
10. Understand and involve diverse users in design decisions.

implementation_examples.description: Students compare two large language models trained primarily on different linguistic or cultural datasets. Using a common set of prompts about culturally specific topics, they analyze differences in tone, emphasis, completeness, and potential bias in the responses. Students then explain how training data and cultural context influence the user experience and suggest ways the system could better support diverse users.

Students analyze how an AI-powered consumer tool (e.g., recommendation engine, translation tool, voice assistant) responds to queries representing different user characteristics (e.g., regional dialects, multilingual prompts, or culturally specific topics). They compare differences in accuracy, tone, and relevance of responses and examine how these variations affect user experience. Students then explain how training data and design choices influence these outcomes and propose ways to improve inclusivity.

standards.statement: Assess how unauthorized data collection has influenced the practice of training AI models.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should evaluate the tension between respecting creators' intellectual property rights and the practice of using copyrighted works to train AI models. They should also consider broader forms of unauthorized data collection, such as scraping personal images or collecting user behavior data without consent. Students could debate whether AI companies should obtain permission and provide compensation when training models on copyrighted works, considering arguments about fair use, the transformative nature of AI-generated outputs, and whether scraping publicly accessible content from the internet constitutes legitimate use or infringement.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to cite specific legislation or case law.

practices.practice: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.
2. Respect others' rights and dignity when creating computing technologies.

implementation_examples.description: Students critique a specific case of facial recognition systems trained on large collections of scraped online images without individuals' consent. Using a short case study and a simplified description of the dataset, students verify which types of data were collected, how that data enabled the model to recognize faces across lighting, angles, and demographics, and why this improved performance. Students then assess the consequences of using unauthorized data by explaining how the same model's accuracy, bias, and real-world use might change if it were trained only on smaller, consent-based datasets, and they conclude by recommending clear guidelines for responsible data use in AI training.

Students evaluate how training datasets for generative AI systems have included images, music, text, or other online content collected without clear permission from creators or users. They verify how the use of these datasets influenced the capabilities and development of AI tools and evaluate the concerns raised by artists, writers, or other affected communities. Students then assess how improved consent practices, licensing agreements, or data transparency could influence future AI model training.

standards.statement: Evaluate how ethical implications of AI have changed over time.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should conduct a critical evaluation of AI ethics, appraising how ethical considerations have changed over time. For example, students could assess the ethical concerns surrounding early conceptions of AI (Asimov's Three Laws of Robotics) and rule-based AI systems (concerns about programming errors and logic) and compare them with the ethical implications of contemporary AI systems that focus on bias, fairness, and transparency. Students should also evaluate ethical challenges that may emerge as AI capabilities advance, drawing from futuristic depictions of AI in media or their own imaginations. Students should communicate their evaluation clearly, articulating how ethical concerns have shifted and presenting a reasoned perspective on emerging challenges.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to conduct research on AI development trajectories or apply specific ethical frameworks. Students are not expected to rigorously define consciousness or sentience in discussions of future AI capabilities.

practices.practice: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.

implementation_examples.description: Students assess how ethical concerns in a specific AI application (e.g., autonomous vehicles, AI-assisted medical diagnosis) have changed over time. They evaluate early debates about reliability or programming errors, along with current concerns about bias, transparency, and accountability in modern AI systems. Students then articulate how ethical considerations may continue to change as these technologies become more widely used and propose ethical guidelines to mitigate those future risks.

Students assess portrayals of AI in media from different time periods and compare them with real-world AI technologies. They evaluate how concerns depicted in earlier stories (e.g., loss of control, machine autonomy) differ from contemporary issues such as data privacy, bias, and misinformation. Students then support how public perceptions of AI ethics may influence future policy or technology development.

standards.statement: Analyze problems that can be addressed using unsupervised learning.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should analyze and categorize the types of real-world problems that can be effectively addressed using unsupervised learning approaches. They should categorize problem characteristics that make unsupervised learning appropriate (e.g., lack of labeled data, need to discover hidden patterns, exploratory data analysis) and provide examples of problem types (e.g., customer segmentation, anomaly detection, dimensionality reduction, pattern discovery in large datasets).
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to implement unsupervised learning algorithms or prove their mathematical convergence properties.

implementation_examples.description: Students work in teams to examine solutions for a business that has accumulated a large, unclassified dataset.  They distinguish the core problem (e.g., grouping customers with similar purchasing patterns, identifying unusual transactions), propose a specific unsupervised learning model, and justify their choice by explaining how the model's function addresses the problem, providing a rationale for why a supervised model would be inappropriate or impossible.

Students analyze a large dataset of environmental observations collected from sensors in a national park (e.g., temperature, humidity, animal activity). They examine how unsupervised learning methods could identify patterns in the data (e.g., grouping similar environmental conditions or detecting unusual activity patterns). Students then contextualize why an unsupervised approach is appropriate when labeled outcomes are not available.

standards.statement: Optimize an AI algorithm's performance for a given problem.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should optimize the performance of a pre-existing AI algorithm or model for a given problem by modifying and tuning the parameters and structures of the algorithm or model. This involves actively altering the algorithm's control flow or hyperparameters, not simply using preset tools. For example, students might optimize an algorithm used in discriminative systems (e.g., by changing the depth of a decision tree used for an image classifier) or adjust the sampling parameters of a generative system. Students could work across different problem domains employing different optimization approaches, such as tuning weights for sentiment analysis, modifying neural network layers for image recognition, or adjusting model parameters for a recommendation system.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to implement algorithms from scratch, work with production-scale systems, or optimize across all possible hyperparameters using advanced techniques (e.g., Bayesian optimization, neural architecture search).

implementation_examples.description: Students optimize a model for a financial workforce problem by predicting whether small loan applications should be approved or denied (binary classification). After training an initial model on historical data, they evaluate its performance and iteratively adjust parameters (e.g., learning rate) and model design to improve reliability. Students also assess the model to balance predictive accuracy with fairness across applicant groups.

Students optimize a model that classifies movie reviews as positive or negative using a labeled dataset. After training an initial model, they iteratively adjust parameters (e.g., number of epochs, learning rate) and evaluate how these changes affect accuracy and error patterns. Students evaluate the results to refine the model and explain how parameter tuning improves performance and reliability.

standards.statement: Create an application using complex supervised learning models.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should design and develop an application that integrates complex supervised learning models to solve a real-world problem. Complex supervised learning models are defined as using more advanced model structures (e.g., random forests, neural networks), larger or richer feature sets, and multiple layers or decision paths. The design and development process includes selecting an appropriate model type (e.g., neural networks, ensemble methods, advanced regression and classification techniques), preparing and preprocessing labeled data, and training the model using suitable tools or libraries. Students should incorporate the trained model into an end-to-end application (e.g., a web app, mobile app, interactive tool) that accepts user input, performs inference, and returns predictions in a usable form. For example, students could create a home price prediction application, select relevant features from housing data (e.g., square footage, location, number of bedrooms), train a supervised learning model, and evaluate its performance by testing predictions against actual prices using appropriate metrics.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to design or implement deep learning models.

implementation_examples.description: Students develop a classification application using complex models to address a problem of interest to them or the workforce (e.g., to predict customer churn [whether a customer will stop using a service], to classify email messages as spam or not spam based on content features, to identify whether a loan applicant is high-risk or low-risk using factors such as credit history, income range, and payment behavior).

Students create (or select) a large, high-dimensional dataset (e.g., customer demographics, usage statistics, support call history) and construct meaningful program features from existing data to strengthen model performance. They design and develop an appropriate complex supervised learning model, program it using standard tools or libraries, and train it on their prepared, labeled dataset. Students formulate an evaluation approach using metrics appropriate for the classification task, iterating on their model as needed. Finally, they create an end-to-end application that accepts user input, performs inference, and returns predictions in a usable form.

standards.statement: Evaluate metadata and data pipelines to support transparency in AI model selection and deployment.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should critically evaluate the entire data pipeline from acquisition through cleaning for potential sources of bias, inaccuracy, and lack of transparency. Students should use this appraisal to justify or critique the selection of a specific AI model and its deployment context. For example, students could evaluate the metadata of an image dataset used to train a facial recognition model (e.g., date of collection, sensor type, demographic coverage), identify a lack of demographic diversity, and argue how this flaw necessitates either selecting a different model less sensitive to demographic bias or changing the deployment plan (e.g., limiting its use to controlled environments).
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to design and implement algorithmic fairness metrics.

practices.practice: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.

implementation_examples.description: Students examine documentation for an AI system used to support small business loan decisions, including dataset descriptions, metadata records, and a diagram of the data pipeline from collection through model input. They critique potential sources of bias, inaccuracy, or lack of transparency in the data pipeline (e.g., missing demographic coverage documentation, unclear labeling practices) and evaluate how these issues affect trust in the model's recommendations. Students then justify whether the system should continue to be used as deployed, supplemented with additional oversight, or limited to specific contexts.

Students evaluate the data pipeline behind an AI system that flags potentially harmful social media posts for human moderators. Using metadata and documentation about how the training data was collected and labeled (e.g., public posts from a limited set of platforms), they assess potential sources of bias, gaps in coverage, or unclear labeling practices. Students then defend whether the system's current deployment is appropriate or argue whether additional safeguards or improved data documentation are needed.

standards.statement: Transform data to meet the input requirements of AI algorithms.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should apply data transformation and restructuring techniques to prepare data for AI algorithms, including feature scaling, handling categorical data, aggregating data, and reshaping data. For example, students could take a raw dataset with mixed feature types and apply normalization to numerical columns and one-hot encoding to categorical columns to prepare the data for a specific algorithm (e.g., k-nearest neighbors classifier).
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to implement dimensionality reduction techniques.

implementation_examples.description: Students transform a customer behavior dataset that includes numerical values (e.g., age, purchase amount) and categorical values (e.g., loyalty status, gender) to meet the input requirements of a selected AI algorithm. Using an IDE and a library, they scale numerical values and encode categorical variables so the data is in a format the algorithm can process.

Students transform a sports performance dataset for use in an AI model by scaling numerical features (e.g., points scored, minutes played, reaction time) and encoding categorical data (e.g., player position, team, home vs. away) into machine-readable formats. They may also restructure the dataset by aggregating player statistics by game or season so the data aligns with the input structure required by the chosen AI algorithm.

standards.statement: Develop policies that promote transparency in AI applications.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should develop a well-reasoned, actionable, and specific policy recommendation aimed at increasing transparency across the AI lifecycle, from raw data to deployed impact, and justify how that policy balances competing values like innovation and privacy. For example, students could draft a policy requiring that high-risk AI applications (e.g., in hiring, in criminal justice) publicly disclose the training data sources, the model type, and the results of a bias analysis before deployment.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to cite existing state or federal statutes or implement the technical infrastructure (e.g., secure data vaults) required to make sensitive data accessible. Students are not expected to produce policy documents that meet professional or legal standards.

practices.practice: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.
10. Understand and involve diverse users in design decisions.

implementation_examples.description: Students investigate how little information is publicly available about an AI system used to screen university admissions applications, including the data used, the model selected, and its impacts on applicants. They then design a policy proposal requiring (a) a data provenance disclosure (which data was used and why), (b) a model rationale statement (why a specific model architecture was chosen over alternatives), and (c) an impact assessment publication explaining who is positively and negatively affected by the AI's use in plain language. Students formulate how these transparency requirements would improve accountability while still allowing the system to be used.

Students examine an AI system used in a real-world decision-making context (e.g., tenant screening for rental housing, automated scheduling for hourly workers) and visualize transparency gaps related to data sources, decision criteria, or impacts on affected groups. They then construct a policy proposal brief that outlines clear public disclosure requirements about how the AI system works and who may benefit or be harmed by its use.

standards.statement: Analyze how model optimization choices impact a model's performance, interpretability, and fairness.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should analyze how different optimization choices (e.g., using gradient descent, adding regularization) and accuracy measures (e.g., F1-score, mean absolute error) affect how an AI model performs and how those choices can impact fairness and interpretability. For example, students could compare how a loan approval model focused only on high recall might lead to more defaults in certain groups, whereas one focused only on high precision might unfairly reject qualified applicants.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to write code or calculate complex metrics.

practices.practice: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.

implementation_examples.description: Students compare two versions of a binary classification model (e.g., to identify spam, to classify medical images), one optimized for precision and one optimized for recall. Using provided performance metrics and a dataset that includes a known bias affecting a protected group, they analyze how different optimization goals affect model accuracy and outcomes for different groups within the dataset. Students then examine how optimization choices can create trade-offs between performance and fairness.

Students analyze a simple classification model (e.g., an image, a text classifier) and how changing model settings (e.g., decision thresholds, model complexity) affects the performance of an AI system used in a real-world context, such as content moderation or fraud detection. Using provided performance metrics, they examine how different configurations influence accuracy, speed, and consistency of predictions. Students then articulate how these optimization choices create trade-offs between performance, interpretability, and fairness and which configuration would be most appropriate for a specific deployment context (e.g., real-time content moderation vs. offline data analysis).

standards.statement: Develop an AI agent to accomplish a defined task.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should design, develop, and optimize an AI agent by setting a clear goal, choosing the information it can use and defining simple steps for how it responds and takes actions. They should develop the agent using an accessible tool and optimize it by testing on a set of realistic prompts.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to build custom AI models for their workflow.

implementation_examples.description: Students design and develop a simple AI agent to address a personally meaningful need (e.g., study support, budgeting, managing communications), defining the agent's goals, inputs, and outputs and assembling prepared or selected data. They program the agent using appropriate models or logic, then test it with realistic scenarios and devise improvements by adjusting parameters, refining inputs or features, and improving decision logic across versions. Students formulate justifications for their optimization choices and document design decisions, development steps, testing results, and any use of AI-assisted tools throughout the process.

Students design an AI agent that helps users navigate a school or community resource, selecting a goal such as helping new students understand school policies, locate academic support services, or find information about extracurricular activities or graduation requirements. They assemble the information the agent will use (e.g., a school handbook, FAQ document, curated links) and construct simple decision steps for responding to user questions. After developing the agent using an accessible AI tool, students plan and execute realistic prompt tests, refine its responses, and document their design choices, testing results and improvements made to increase accuracy and usefulness.

standards.statement: Develop professional communications by interpreting technical AI results for diverse audiences.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should develop professional communications by translating model performance metrics (e.g., F1-score, precision, recall) and ethical risks (e.g., disparate impact, bias) into language that is relevant and actionable for specific nontechnical audiences. For example, students could create a presentation on an AI-driven school admissions model where the executive summary for the school board focuses on cost-savings and scalability, and the community group briefing focuses on fairness metrics and due process for appeals.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to create publishable graphics or animated media or to participate in real-world communications campaigns.

practices.practice: 10. Understand and involve diverse users in design decisions.

implementation_examples.description: Students create three distinct communication artifacts for an AI model they previously developed: a written policy brief for a policymaker summarizing regulatory compliance and risk, a presentation for a community group that uses analogies and visual aids to explain how the model works and its impact on daily life, and a script for an executive that uses business language (e.g., "ROI," "risk mitigation") to justify a recommendation to deploy or discontinue the project. Each artifact is assessed on clarity, accuracy, and appropriate adaptation of tone and vocabulary for its specific audience.

Students adapt results from an AI system they have studied or built into three communication formats for different audiences: a one-page technical summary for a peer developer covering model performance (e.g., accuracy, common errors, limitations), an infographic or short explainer video for the general public describing what the system does and how reliable it is, and a composed email or slide memo for a school or organizational leader highlighting benefits, risks, and recommended next steps. Students are assessed on how well they design each artifact to adjust language, structure, and emphasis for each audience while preserving the accuracy of the AI results.

standards.statement: Debate aspects of AI regulatory frameworks and legislation across countries.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should assess major AI regulatory frameworks from at least two regions of the world (e.g., the European Union's AI Act [EU AI Act] vs. a US state or federal approach). Students should critique the core philosophical approaches and practical impacts on key areas like data sovereignty and governance. For example, students could assess how the EU's focus on regulating "high-risk" AI systems differs from a less restrictive regulatory environment and debate the resulting impact on innovation speed versus human protections in areas like facial recognition.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to read the text of legislation.

practices.practice: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.

implementation_examples.description: Students appraise two different legislative approaches: one emphasizing a right to explanation in automated decisions (e.g., an element of the GDPR or similar law) and another emphasizing a flexible, industry-led approach (e.g., a proposed US framework). They engage in a structured policy debate where one side argues that the regulation (e.g., the EU AI Act) stifles innovation and limits the utility of complex models, and the other side argues that the regulation is necessary to safeguard fundamental rights like privacy and nondiscrimination. Students must defend their position by addressing trade-offs between promoting technological advancement and ensuring strong human protections in the use of AI.

Students participate in a policy workshop examining how different countries regulate AI systems. They work in groups representing different regions to assess how each regulatory approach addresses issues such as innovation, transparency, and human rights protections. Using a shared scenario (e.g., deploying facial recognition, automated hiring tools), students debate whether and how the technology should be regulated under different national frameworks and justify their group's recommended approach.

standards.statement: Analyze the role of network services and protocols in secure communication and their potential vulnerabilities.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should analyze security trade-offs in common network services and protocols based on context, including when plaintext communication may be acceptable and when encryption is required. Analysis should include: (a) comparison of insecure versus secure protocol pairs (e.g., HTTP/HTTPS, Telnet/SSH), (b) examination of common vulnerabilities, and (c) contextualizing of risks to users and communities if those vulnerabilities are exploited. Students may demonstrate understanding through simulated environments, packet capture analysis, case studies, or instructor-provided demonstrations.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to exploit live networks, configure enterprise infrastructure, or analyze advanced routing protocols. Hands-on Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) simulations are not required and should only be conducted in safe, isolated environments where permitted.

implementation_examples.description: Students analyze common network services and protocols using scenario cards or system diagrams (e.g., web browsing, email, file transfer). For each scenario, they classify the protocols involved and articulate their purpose in communication. Students then detect potential vulnerabilities (e.g., unencrypted data transmission, reliance on weak authentication) and explain how these weaknesses could be exploited, emphasizing reasoning about security risks without requiring live network access.

Students examine simplified network traffic logs or protocol summaries generated from a simulated environment. They distinguish which services and protocols are in use and analyze how each contributes to secure or insecure communication. Students articulate how protocol design choices (e.g., encryption support, lack of authentication) affect vulnerability exposure, then summarize their findings in a short analysis connecting protocol function to security implications.

standards.statement: Examine the concepts of the Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) model and their role in network communication.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should trace the path of a data packet through the OSI model, articulating how data is encapsulated and processed at each layer during transmission. Students should use the OSI model as a tool for reasoning, troubleshooting, and security analysis, not rote memorization. Students should identify which layers support key security functions, such as encryption, authentication, or error detection. Students should demonstrate a functional understanding of how layered systems support connectivity and security.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to memorize all protocol-layer mappings or perform low-level debugging. Students are not expected to recall the exact sequence of all seven layers or associate every protocol with its specific layer.

implementation_examples.description: Students participate in a layered communication activity in which a message is broken into stages representing the OSI model layers. They model specific communication tasks (e.g., formatting data, addressing, error handling) to the appropriate layer, then examine how separating communication into layers supports interoperability, troubleshooting, and system design.

Students analyze a real-world communication scenario, such as accessing a website or sending a message across a network. They trace which OSI layers are involved at each stage of communication and articulate the role each layer plays. Students represent their analysis using diagrams, annotated workflows, or written narratives to demonstrate layered reasoning rather than memorization.

standards.statement: Distinguish between networks based on their protocols, topologies, and addressing schemes.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should distinguish between common network architectures (wired, wireless, hybrid) and articulate how topologies, segmentation and addressing schemes, and protocols interact in real-world systems. Students should analyze how modern networks: (a) combine multiple topologies (e.g., hybrid, mesh), (b) use multiple protocols simultaneously, and (c) employ IPv4 and IPv6 addressing.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to rigidly classify networks into single categories. For example, students are not expected to classify networks into legacy addressing classes (e.g., Class A, Class B, Class C), but rather to describe how addressing is structured and used within a network. Students are not expected to design complex addressing plans or configure production networks.

implementation_examples.description: Students examine diagrams and descriptions of different network environments (e.g., a home network, a school network, a small office). For each network, they distinguish the topology (e.g., centralized, hierarchical, distributed), the communication protocols in use, and the IP addressing structure, including how devices are identified, whether addresses are private or public, and how addressing supports communication within the network. Students articulate how these characteristics influence network organization, communication flow, and basic security considerations.

Students analyze simplified network configuration summaries or simulated network models, articulating each network's topology, communication protocols, and IP addressing structure. They examine how addressing enables devices to communicate locally or externally, then compare multiple networks and articulate how differences in structure affect scalability or management.

standards.statement: Examine security risks in digital systems and corresponding mitigation strategies.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should analyze cybersecurity risks by identifying threats, vulnerabilities, exploits, and potential impacts using a simple risk framework that considers likelihood and impact. Students may analyze case studies or simulated scenarios to: (a) identify risks (including AI-enhanced threats, such as automated phishing), (b) propose appropriate mitigation strategies, and (c) evaluate societal impacts, including effects on trust, equity, or access to services. Hands-on investigation may occur in isolated virtual environments, such as a cyber range, or through instructor-provided artifacts.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to conduct penetration testing or deploy enterprise security tools. Students are not expected to access physical hardware or live networks.

implementation_examples.description: Students analyze a set of digital system scenarios (e.g., a school network, a personal device, a small business system). For each scenario, they articulate potential security risks, including weak passwords, unpatched software, or unsecured network access. Students then analyze appropriate mitigation strategies (e.g., stronger authentication practices, software updates, access controls) and attribute how each mitigation reduces risk without significantly impacting usability.

Students examine system descriptions, logs, or simplified security reports from a simulated environment and detect indicators of security risks (e.g., repeated failed login attempts, exposed services). They correlate each identified risk to a corresponding mitigation strategy and articulate why that strategy is effective, focusing on analyzing threats and defenses rather than executing attacks.

standards.statement: Apply diagnostic tools and techniques to resolve network connectivity issues.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should use basic network diagnostic tools to document connectivity and performance issues and to investigate whether those issues may indicate misconfiguration, failure, or potential security concerns. At a minimum, students should: (a) use command-line or equivalent diagnostic tools (e.g., ping, traceroute, netstat, simulated equivalents), (b) connect observed behavior to relevant OSI layers to isolate where a problem may be occurring, and (c) document whether issues are due to routine network issues (e.g., latency, packet loss, routing failures) or whether they may indicate security-related events, such as denial-of-service activity or on-path interference. Students should focus on systematic troubleshooting, evidence-based reasoning, and understanding the security implications of network behavior.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to have access to system-level permissions or live network monitoring tools. Students are not expected to write diagnostic scripts, perform penetration testing, deploy monitoring infrastructure, or respond to live attacks. Students are not expected to perform operational remediation.

implementation_examples.description: Students are presented with a network connectivity problem, such as a device that cannot access local resources or the internet. Using basic diagnostic tools (e.g., checking network status, testing connectivity, reviewing IP configuration), they systematically investigate the source of the issue. Students document the troubleshooting steps they used and explain how each step helped narrow down the problem before applying a solution.

Students work through a structured troubleshooting scenario involving a simulated or real network setup. They apply diagnostic techniques such as verifying physical connections, confirming device configuration, and testing communication paths, explaining their reasoning at each step. Students reflect on how a methodical troubleshooting process improves efficiency and accuracy when resolving connectivity issues.

standards.statement: Analyze system processes and network activity using command-line tools to identify potential security concerns.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should analyze system or network activity to identify potential security concerns, using a defensive and ethical perspective. At a minimum, students should: (a) explain why systems generate logs (e.g., accountability, troubleshooting, security), (b) identify common indicators of concern in logs or monitoring outputs (e.g., repeated failed logins, unusual process activity, unexpected network connections), and (c) propose appropriate mitigation or response strategies based on observed behavior. Students may examine instructor-provided logs, command outputs, packet summaries, screenshots, or scripted scenarios rather than executing tools directly. When command-line tools (e.g., process listing, system status, network discovery utilities) are used, they should be limited to safe, read-only, defensive contexts within virtualized or sandboxed environments where permitted.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to perform vulnerability scanning, penetration testing, password attacks, exploit development, or unauthorized network scanning. Students are not expected to execute powerful tools (e.g., network scanners) on live or unauthorized networks.

implementation_examples.description: Students use command-line tools to audit a computer system by listing running processes, checking active network connections, and reviewing system resource usage. They investigate the output to identify unusual or unnecessary processes and explain how these could indicate misconfiguration or security concerns. Students produce documentation of their observations and recommended basic actions (e.g., disabling unused services, monitoring specific activity).

Students analyze simulated scan results or network inspection reports provided by the instructor. They examine scan results to document outdated software, open ports, or configuration weaknesses. Students connect what results suggest about system security and discuss appropriate next steps (e.g., applying updates, limiting network exposure) without attempting exploitation.

standards.statement: Analyze how common cyber threats related to network activity exploit system vulnerabilities.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should analyze how common cyber threats exploit vulnerabilities in digital systems, with particular attention to network-related examples, and distinguish clearly between threats, vulnerabilities, exploits, and attacks. Students should analyze examples such as spoofing, interception, denial-of-service, or misuse of insecure protocols to articulate: (a) what the threat is, (b) what vulnerability is being targeted, and (c) what impact the attack could have on users or communities. Students should focus on developing conceptual understanding, classification, and explanation.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to perform attacks, exploit systems, or simulate adversarial behavior. Students are not expected to use offensive security tools or reproduce attack techniques in any environment.

practices.practice: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.

implementation_examples.description: Students examine case studies or incident summaries describing network-based cyber threats (e.g., phishing campaigns, denial-of-service activity, unauthorized access attempts). They analyze the vulnerabilities that were exploited (e.g., weak authentication, exposed services) and articulate how the threat leveraged network activity to succeed. Students correlate each threat to prevention or mitigation strategies.

Students analyze logs, alerts, or simplified network activity records from a simulated system experiencing suspicious behavior. They detect patterns associated with common cyber threats (e.g., repeated connection attempts, unexpected data transfers) and articulate how these behaviors exploit underlying vulnerabilities. Students evaluate the potential impact on system confidentiality, integrity, or availability.

standards.statement: Evaluate a security threat using the CIA triad, states of data, and types of control.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should evaluate common cybersecurity threats based on their impact on the confidentiality, integrity, and availability properties of an information system. Students should evaluate specific, common threat examples (e.g., ransomware, malware, denial-of-service attacks, on-path attacks) using the CIA model and assess: (a) which CIA properties are affected, (b) which data states are impacted (data at rest, in transit, or in use), and (c) which types of security controls (preventive, detective, or corrective) are most relevant. Students should focus on structured reasoning, classification, and explanation.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to design security systems, implement controls, or analyze advanced threat models. Students are not expected to select or deploy specific security products or technologies.

implementation_examples.description: Students evaluate a set of security incident scenarios (e.g., data breaches, service outages, unauthorized access events). For each scenario, they assess the primary impact using the CIA triad, map the state of data involved (at rest, in transit, or in use), and appraise which types of control (administrative, technical, or physical) could mitigate the threat. Students justify their classifications using evidence from the scenario.

Students review logs, alerts, or case study summaries from simulated digital systems. They evaluate observed threats according to the CIA triad, map how each threat affects data at different states, and assess relevant controls that could reduce risk. Students appraise multiple incidents to identify patterns in how threats impact systems and how layered controls improve security posture.

standards.statement: Analyze how encryption methods in network communication protect privacy and security.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should analyze how symmetric and asymmetric encryption methods support confidentiality, integrity, authentication, and nonrepudiation in digital systems and articulate when encryption is necessary based on context. Students should evaluate established, trusted cryptographic algorithms and libraries. Students should analyze trade-offs associated with encryption, including: (a) performance and computational overhead, (b) key management complexity, and (c) situations where plaintext communication may be acceptable or preferable. Students should understand at a conceptual level that encryption strength varies and that some methods require significantly more computational effort to break than others.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to implement cryptographic algorithms, break encryption, or evaluate algorithmic strength mathematically. Students are not expected to analyze the mathematical foundations of cryptographic hardness or assess how advances in computing (e.g., quantum computing) may impact specific algorithms.

practices.practice: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.

implementation_examples.description: Students analyze common encryption scenarios (e.g., sending a secure email, making an online purchase, accessing a password-protected account) and identify whether symmetric or asymmetric encryption is used in each case. For each scenario, they articulate which CIA properties are protected, evaluate the trade-offs involved (e.g., performance vs. security strength), and justify whether the level of encryption is appropriate for the context.

Students compare encrypted and unencrypted communication scenarios (e.g., HTTP vs. HTTPS, unencrypted vs. encrypted messaging applications). They analyze which information is protected in each case, identify which users or communities are most affected when encryption is absent, and articulate why stronger encryption requires more computational effort to break. Students evaluate when plaintext communication may be acceptable and when encryption is necessary to protect privacy and security.

standards.statement: Evaluate security measures as part of a layered defense strategy to protect sensitive information.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should evaluate common security controls by categorizing them as preventive, detective, or corrective and assessing their use as part of a layered defense strategy. Students should consider security controls across multiple domains (e.g., network security such as firewalls and filtering, application security such as input validation and authentication, device and system security such as updates and access controls, and physical security such as locks and secured locations). Students should understand that no single control is sufficient on its own and that effective cybersecurity relies on multiple, overlapping layers of defense (defense-in-depth). Students should also evaluate trade-offs and constraints associated with security controls, such as ease of use versus strength of protection, cost and complexity, and impact on productivity or accessibility.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to configure security tools, deploy AI systems, or implement enterprise-grade defenses. Students are not expected to select or configure specific commercial security products.

practices.practice: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.

implementation_examples.description: Students examine scenarios involving sensitive information (e.g., student records, medical data, financial information). For each scenario, they classify the types of data involved and describe appropriate security measures (e.g., access controls, authentication methods, encryption, physical safeguards). Students explain how each measure helps protect confidentiality and reduces the risk of unauthorized access.

Students analyze a digital system or workflow (e.g., an online form, a shared file system, an internal database). They describe which security measures are in place or should be in place to protect sensitive information and explain why each is necessary. Students differentiate between multiple measures and discuss trade-offs between security, usability, and accessibility.

standards.statement: Explain the importance of cybersecurity policies in protecting organizational assets and mitigating risks.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should explain the purpose of cybersecurity policies and how they translate legal, ethical, and organizational requirements into clear, actionable rules that guide user behavior and protect systems, data, and people. Students should understand the history of cybersecurity policies at a high level, including why formal security policies emerged as computing systems became networked and widely used, how early failures, breaches, and misuse highlighted the need for governance alongside technical controls, and why policy is an essential but often overlooked component of cybersecurity practice. Students should analyze common categories of organizational cybersecurity policies (e.g., acceptable use policies, data classification and handling policies, access control and password policies, incident reporting policies).
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to draft comprehensive policies or interpret statutes. Students are not expected to evaluate whether specific organizations are in compliance with laws or regulations.

implementation_examples.description: Students review summaries of common cybersecurity policies (e.g., acceptable use policies, password policies, data handling guidelines). They explain how these policies help protect organizational assets, reduce risk, and guide user behavior. Students then discuss what could happen if such policies are absent, unclear, or ignored.

Students analyze a case study involving a cybersecurity incident linked to weak or missing policies. Using provided documentation or incident descriptions, they explain how stronger or better-enforced policies could have mitigated the risk or reduced impact. Students interpret the connection between policy decisions and technical and human factors within the organization.

standards.statement: Explain key components of effective security policies.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should explain the key components of organizational cybersecurity policies (e.g., purpose and scope, roles and responsibilities, acceptable and unacceptable behaviors, enforcement mechanisms, consequences for violations). Students should describe how these components work together to shape user behavior, organizational security, and accountability. Students should demonstrate understanding of policy structure, its social impact, and ethical trade-offs.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to draft full organizational policies or assess legal compliance. Students are not expected to evaluate whether a specific policy meets regulatory requirements or industry standards. Students are not expected to demonstrate legal or administrative expertise.

practices.practice: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.

implementation_examples.description: Students are given summaries or excerpts from different cybersecurity policies (e.g., acceptable use, password management, data handling policies). They identify key components, including purpose, scope, roles and responsibilities, acceptable and unacceptable behaviors, and consequences for violations. Students then list why each component is necessary for an effective policy and name how missing elements could weaken organizational security.

Students analyze a hypothetical organization and review a simplified security policy outline, identifying which essential components are present and which are missing or unclear. They label the inclusion or absence of specific components and state how each affects policy effectiveness, user understanding, and risk mitigation within the organization.

standards.statement: Analyze the potential consequences of cybersecurity decisions on individuals, organizations, and society.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should analyze how cybersecurity decisions involve trade-offs between technical effectiveness, human judgment, and societal impact. Students should examine sociotechnical decision-making scenarios in which technical solutions interact with human behavior, organizational values, and ethical considerations (e.g., automated security responses vs. human-in-the-loop decision-making, predictive threat modeling systems that prioritize certain alerts or users, monitoring systems that improve security but raise privacy or surveillance concerns). Students should demonstrate reasoned analysis, ethical evaluation, and understanding of consequences.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to build AI systems, deploy automated defenses, or perform real-time security operations.

practices.practice: 2. Respect others' rights and dignity when creating computing technologies.

implementation_examples.description: Students analyze scenarios involving cybersecurity decisions (e.g., choosing weaker authentication for convenience, delaying system updates to avoid downtime). They contextualize potential consequences for individuals (privacy loss), organizations (financial or reputational damage), and society (reduced trust in digital systems). Students articulate how short-term decisions can lead to long-term impacts.

Students examine a real or simulated cybersecurity incident and analyze the decisions that led to the outcome. They trace consequences at multiple levels and contrast how alternative choices could have reduced harm. Students contextualize ethical responsibilities in cybersecurity decision-making and justify recommended actions.

standards.statement: Analyze social engineering techniques and how they exploit human cognitive biases and organizational weaknesses.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should analyze and deconstruct common social engineering techniques used to manipulate individuals into revealing information or performing unsafe actions. Students should examine concrete examples of social engineering (e.g., phishing messages, pretexting scenarios, impersonation attempts), identify persuasion techniques used (e.g., urgency, authority, trust, fear), and explain how these techniques exploit human behavior rather than technical flaws. Students should focus on analysis, recognition, and prevention.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to conduct real phishing campaigns, create deceptive content, or exploit others. Students are not expected to design or deploy social engineering techniques.

practices.practice: 12. Design computing technologies that empower and inform users.

implementation_examples.description: Students examine scenario cards describing social engineering attempts (e.g., phishing emails, pretexting phone calls, impersonation incidents). For each scenario, they classify the technique used and explain which cognitive biases (e.g., authority, urgency, trust) or organizational weaknesses (e.g., lack of training, unclear procedures) are being exploited. Students discuss how awareness and policy-based safeguards can reduce risk.

Students analyze simulated messages, screenshots, or incident summaries related to social engineering attacks. They classify indicators of manipulation, explain the psychological or organizational factors involved, and describe preventive measures (e.g., user training, verification procedures, reporting mechanisms). Students interpret how human factors connect to broader cybersecurity risk management.

standards.statement: Translate cybersecurity concepts, risks, and solutions clearly to both technical and nontechnical audiences.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should translate technical cybersecurity information into clear, accurate, and actionable communication for nontechnical audiences. Students should identify the intended audience (e.g., executives, users, community members), distill complex technical findings (e.g., vulnerabilities, risks, incidents) into plain language explanations, and highlight implications, recommendations, and next steps appropriate to the audience's role and level of technical knowledge.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to produce communications for real external stakeholders or organizations. Students should not rely exclusively on AI-generated text.

practices.practice: 10. Understand and involve diverse users in design decisions.

implementation_examples.description: Students create two explanations of the same cybersecurity concept (e.g., phishing risks, password hygiene): one for a technical audience and one for a nontechnical audience. They differentiate vocabulary, depth, and examples to match each audience while preserving accuracy and receive feedback on clarity and effectiveness.

Students present a cybersecurity risk and recommended solution using multiple communication formats, (e.g., brief presentation, infographic, written summary). They explain how their communication choices support understanding for different audiences and discuss the importance of clear communication in promoting secure behavior.

standards.statement: Integrate security features in networking hardware and software.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should integrate and configure security features found in networking hardware (e.g., routers, firewalls, access points) and software (e.g., host-based firewalls, intrusion detection systems, server configurations) to establish defense-in-depth. Configuration tasks may include setting up a VPN tunnel on a router, configuring access control lists on a simulated switch or router, and integrating a host-based firewall on a server. For example, students could use virtual network labs or simulation tools to configure firewall policies that allow access to a server only from a specified subnet and require encrypted communication or authentication protocols.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to physically manipulate hardware, write custom firmware for network devices, or deploy security solutions on networks with real-time production traffic.

implementation_examples.description: Students analyze a small network setup that includes routers, switches, and endpoint devices. They detect available security features (e.g., access controls, firewall rules, authentication settings, logging capabilities), then simulate enabling selected security features and articulate how each contributes to protecting the network from unauthorized access or misuse. Students examine how hardware and software security features work together as part of a layered defense strategy.

Students examine a physical or simulated network environment and outline how security features could be integrated across devices. They distinguish which security controls should be applied at the hardware level (e.g., device access restrictions) versus the software level (e.g., authentication, monitoring), then contextualize their decisions based on threat scenarios and system requirements, demonstrating an understanding of coordinated security integration.

standards.statement: Design a secure network, including servers, switches, routers, endpoints, and firewalls.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should plan security features within a network design to detect, analyze, and respond to suspicious or malicious activity, using a defense-in-depth approach. Students may demonstrate this through scaffolded design exercises, such as configuring traffic monitoring or logging mechanisms and articulating the indicators that might signal abnormal behavior, choosing security controls at multiple layers (e.g., network, endpoint, application), and conceptually designing automated responses (e.g., alerting, blocking traffic, isolating compromised components). Students should configure security features appropriately, reason about trade-offs, and explain how design choices improve security rather than pursuing exhaustive implementation.
