standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to design or deploy fully optimized control systems, implement complex control algorithms, perform exhaustive quantitative analyses across multiple sensor dimensions, or build systems requiring specialized hardware, industrial-grade components, or mission-critical reliability.

practices.practice: 10. Understand and involve diverse users in design decisions.
12. Design computing technologies that empower and inform users.

implementation_examples.description: Students design a closed-loop control system to regulate temperature using a physical computing device. They devise criteria for selecting temperature sensors based on accuracy, response time, and reliability. Students program software that continuously compares sensor readings to a target value and adjusts an actuator, such as a fan or heater, to maintain the desired temperature, then iterates on the feedback logic to minimize overshoot and instability.

Students develop a closed-loop system to control motor speed (e.g., maintaining a constant conveyor speed) or position (e.g., stabilizing a robotic arm joint). They generate selection criteria for sensor types, such as encoders or distance sensors, based on system requirements. Students program and iterate on feedback control strategies, generating insights into how sensor choice and control logic affect system performance and reliability.

standards.statement: Develop an application that extends functionality and user engagement with physical devices.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should develop applications that extend how users interact with physical systems, such as configuration options, feedback displays, data-informed behavior, or app-connected interaction. Students should focus on clarity of design, user interaction, and purposeful extension of functionality.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to implement fully autonomous systems, advanced control algorithms, multilayer feedback architectures, or professional-grade embedded software pipelines.

practices.practice: 10. Understand and involve diverse users in design decisions.

implementation_examples.description: Students develop a user-facing application that interacts with a physical computing device, such as a dashboard that displays real-time sensor data and allows users to adjust system settings. They design the application to extend the device's functionality through configuration, monitoring, or control via a graphical interface, then evaluate how it improves usability and user engagement compared to device-only interaction.

Students design an interactive application that enhances engagement with a physical device, such as a mobile or desktop interface for a smart appliance or assistive technology. They develop features that allow users to visualize system behavior, receive alerts, or customize responses, then refine the application based on user feedback, demonstrating how software design enhances the overall system experience.

standards.statement: Develop IoT systems to manage the collection and transmission of data and enable remote monitoring and control of physical systems.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should develop IoT systems that transmit, receive, and use data across connected physical devices, using communication structures appropriate to the application. Connectivity may be local or extended, and students should justify communication choices based on range, latency, data size, power use, or reliability. Systems may be conceptual, simulated, or implemented, depending on instructional context.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to deploy enterprise-scale IoT platforms or manage persistent cloud infrastructure.

practices.practice: 10. Understand and involve diverse users in design decisions.

implementation_examples.description: Students develop an IoT-enabled system that collects sensor data from a physical device and transmits it to a remote interface for monitoring. They program the system to allow users to view real-time or logged data and send control commands back to the device. Students plan communication reliability tests and visualize how remote access improves system effectiveness and responsiveness.

Students design a remote monitoring and control solution for a physical system such as environmental sensing, automated irrigation, or equipment status tracking. The IoT devices collect data and transmit it to a remote user interface, enabling oversight and intervention without direct physical access. Students formulate conclusions about trade-offs related to latency, reliability, and user needs when operating systems remotely.

standards.statement: Develop an embedded network, evaluating trade-offs among network protocols, security measures, and scalability.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should coordinate data from multiple physical devices using centralized or distributed approaches. Central coordination might be implemented using a local computer, single-board device, or simple script. Students might design simple communication protocols and reason about message structure and flow. Communication might be simulated or implemented, depending on instructional context. Students should connect networking and security concepts to physical system behavior.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not required to use cloud servers or web services. Students are not expected to implement advanced cryptographic protocols, perform detailed packet-level analysis, configure enterprise security systems, or master low-level networking theory.

implementation_examples.description: Students design and implement a small embedded network consisting of multiple physical computing devices that communicate to share sensor data. They evaluate different communication protocols (e.g., wired vs. wireless, short-range options vs. longer-range options) and justify their selection based on performance, reliability, and ease of implementation. Students secure the network using basic measures such as authentication or access restrictions, then assess how protocol and security choices affect network scalability and system complexity.

Students plan and test an embedded network for a real-world use case, such as environmental monitoring across a building or coordinated control of multiple devices. They evaluate network designs by examining trade-offs related to data throughput, security requirements, device count, and future expansion. Students justify their design decisions and assess how changes in scale or security needs would impact the network architecture.

standards.statement: Apply project management methodologies to design, develop, and test physical computing projects collaboratively.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should apply project management methodologies (e.g., agile frameworks) to collaboratively manage a physical computing project from conception through delivery. They should share responsibilities, resolve conflicts equitably, and communicate progress and outcomes. For example, students might use a Kanban board to track tasks (e.g., prototyping, circuit design, programming the microcontroller, user testing) and hold regular stand-up meetings to discuss progress and resolve issues.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to use professional project management software or lead projects with multiple teams and external stakeholders.

implementation_examples.description: Students work in teams to complete a physical computing project using a defined project management framework, such as task boards or milestone planning. Teams assign roles, set timelines, track progress, and document testing results as they design and build a physical computing solution. Students reflect on how project management practices supported risk reduction and timely completion of the project.

Students use a shared digital project management tool to plan and coordinate the development of a physical computing system. Tasks such as circuit construction, software development, and testing are tracked through assigned responsibilities and deadlines. Students document assigned responsibilities and deadlines across multiple tasks (e.g., circuit construction, software development, testing) and update project artifacts as issues arise and revisions are made. Students reflect on how structured project management supports effective coordination and system refinement.

standards.statement: Evaluate how physical computing technologies shape social processes, communities, power, and equity in global society.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should evaluate how physical computing systems shape social, technical, and human outcomes through specific design decisions in their projects. Students might conduct small-scale, local research (e.g., surveys, interviews, observations) to identify relevant problems. Evaluation should focus on one or two impact dimensions (e.g., accessibility, sustainability, safety) and include a clear viability criterion such as cost, usability, or maintenance.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to conduct formal sociological studies or global policy analysis.

practices.practice: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.
2. Respect others' rights and dignity when creating computing technologies.

implementation_examples.description: Students evaluate case studies involving physical computing technologies, such as sensor-based surveillance systems, automated public infrastructure, or assistive devices. They assess how these technologies influence access, privacy, decision-making power, and equity within communities. Students critique who benefits, who could be marginalized, and how design choices can reinforce or reduce existing inequities.

Students evaluate a physical computing solution deployed in a global or community context, such as environmental monitoring in developing regions or automated systems in urban environments. They assess social and sociotechnical impacts, including economic access, cultural considerations, and governance. Students defend design or policy changes that would promote more equitable outcomes while maintaining technical feasibility.

standards.statement: Develop physical computing solutions for diverse users using the engineering design process.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should develop physical computing solutions using the engineering design process to plan, build, test, and refine a physical computing project. The process should be evidenced through design sketches, written plans, testing notes, and reflections tied directly to technical decisions. Students should demonstrate an awareness of the needs of diverse users and address them in the design process.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to follow formal project management frameworks or use professional version control systems.

practices.practice: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.
10. Understand and involve diverse users in design decisions.

implementation_examples.description: Students work in teams to design a physical computing solution that addresses a real-world need for a specific user group, such as an accessibility aid or environmental monitoring device. Teams follow the engineering design process by defining the problem, identifying user needs, brainstorming solutions, building prototypes, testing functionality, and iterating based on feedback. Students document how design decisions change in response to user constraints, usability concerns, or testing results, demonstrating effective problem-solving and refinement.

Students work in teams to design and simulate a physical computing system using a digital environment or shared coding platform. Team members divide responsibilities for circuit design, code development, and system testing. Using the engineering design process, students refine their solution based on simulated performance data and peer feedback, ensuring that the final design meets the needs of diverse users while functioning as intended.

standards.statement: Implement linear data structures to organize and access collections of data when solving computational problems.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should select appropriate linear data structures to store and manage data to solve a computational problem. Students should use arrays for fixed-size collections accessed by position, dynamic arrays (lists) for collections that grow or shrink, linked lists for efficient insertion and deletion, stacks for last-in-first-out access, and queues for first-in-first-out access. For example, students could use a dynamic array to store temperature readings collected over time, a stack to implement an undo feature in an application, or a queue to manage print jobs in the order they were submitted. Students should use built-in APIs or libraries and their associated methods.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to implement these data structures or their operations (e.g., insert, delete, search) from scratch. Students are not expected to use dictionaries, trees, graphs, or heaps.

implementation_examples.description: Students write a program to manage a digital music collection. The program reads a list of songs from a file, storing the song titles in a dynamic array to maintain a playlist order. The program allows users to sort the playlist, search for words within a title, add new song titles, and remove song titles, demonstrating students' abilities to use linear data structures and their associated APIs and libraries.

Students implement a simple school tech help desk system to manage support requests submitted by users. Incoming requests are stored in a queue to ensure they are handled in the order received, and active tickets being worked on are tracked in a dynamic array that can grow and shrink as tickets are opened and closed.

standards.statement: Design software that accounts for complexity through abstraction.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should apply design principles that promote maintainable and extensible software. Students should make intentional decisions about program structure, data organization, and relationships between components. They should consider how their software will handle growth (e.g., more users, more data, more features) and apply abstraction (e.g., data abstractions, procedural abstraction, recursion, object-oriented abstraction) to manage complexity. For example, students could design a social media application that organizes data efficiently to support adding more users and posts without rewriting core functionality.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to handle scalability challenges requiring specialized infrastructure (e.g., multiple servers, distributed databases). Students are not expected to perform algorithm complexity analysis or optimize code for speed and memory usage.

implementation_examples.description: Student groups develop a text-based adventure game with multiple characters, a player inventory, and different locations. The complexity of the project, including the potential for expansion (scalability), is managed through object-oriented programming (OOP). The students create base classes for Character, Inventory, and Location, which are abstracted into subclasses as needed. By using these abstractions, the students simplify the code and can add new characters, items, or locations without a major refactoring of the entire program, demonstrating an understanding of scalability and managing complex interactions.

Students design a task-management application that is intentionally structured to support future growth and new features. The program uses clear abstractions to separate concerns, such as defining data abstractions for tasks or events, procedural abstractions for operations like adding or editing entries, and OOP to represent different types of users or tasks. Students assemble data and program components so that new features can be added without rewriting core logic. Students develop a thoughtful program structure that improves maintainability, extensibility, and the ability to manage increasing complexity over time.

standards.statement: Use integrated development environment (IDE) features to streamline software development, including code editing, debugging, version control, and project management.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should use the core features of an IDE to increase their efficiency and effectiveness in developing software. This includes utilizing the IDE's built-in tools for syntax highlighting, autocomplete, and real-time error detection while writing code. Students should use the integrated debugger to set breakpoints, step through code, and inspect variables to diagnose and fix logical errors. Students should also be able to interact with a version control system directly within the IDE to manage changes to their code, commit new versions, and collaborate on projects. Students should also use the IDE's project management features, such as organizing files and folders and managing dependencies, to maintain a structured project.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to deeply understand the underlying mechanisms of these tools (e.g., how the debugger works at a machine level), set up complex IDE configurations from scratch, or configure custom build processes.

implementation_examples.description: Students build a simple text-based adventure game using IDE features (e.g., syntax highlighting, autocomplete) to write their code. When an error occurs, students use the IDE's debugger to set a breakpoint at the relevant line, step through the code, and examine the relevant variable's value to find the source of the problem. Throughout the program development, they use the IDE's integrated version control to commit changes after implementing new features and to revert to a previous version if a new change breaks the program. They also use the IDE to manage all the project files, including source code and game assets, in a well-organized structure.

Students build a small interactive quiz application. While writing code, students use syntax highlighting, autocomplete, and real-time error detection within the IDE to improve code quality and reduce common mistakes. To investigate logical errors, students use the IDE's integrated debugger to set breakpoints, step through program execution, and inspect variable values. Throughout development, students use the IDE's built-in version control tools to execute changes, document revisions, restore earlier versions when needed, and store source files and assets using the IDE's project management features. The assignment emphasizes using IDE tools intentionally to support efficient development, debugging, and long-term project organization.

standards.statement: Refine a user interface design using accessibility and responsive design tools.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should evaluate the effectiveness of user interface design choices in a digital product based on established principles such as contrast, alignment, proximity, and readability. For example, students could analyze a mobile app's user interface using an accessibility design tool and provide a written critique of how element alignment and color contrast affect readability for users with low vision.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to design graphics, nor are they expected to create design systems that specify detailed guidelines for all visual and interaction elements across a product.

practices.practice: 10. Understand and involve diverse users in design decisions.

implementation_examples.description: Students implement a portfolio of design critiques, investigating a variety of mobile applications or websites and write a detailed evaluation of each one's user interface. The critique addresses how well the UI adheres to principles of contrast, alignment, proximity, and readability and proposes specific, human-centered design improvements.

Students evaluate the user interface of a consumer-supporting digital system (e.g., car infotainment display, self-checkout kiosk, smart home control panel). Students analyze specific interface components (e.g., navigation layout, text size, icon grouping, color usage, feedback messages) using established design principles, including contrast, alignment, proximity, and readability. They write a focused critique explaining how these design choices support or hinder usability and accessibility for a range of users and propose concrete design improvements grounded in human-centered design principles.

standards.statement: Create software that serves intended users and contexts using human-centered design principles.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should conduct heuristic reviews (i.e., systematic evaluations against established design criteria such as usability, consistency, accessibility, and user control) to assess how well the software serves diverse users, including variations in ability, language, and cultural context. Students should use these evaluations to inform design decisions and recommendations.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to conduct user testing or collect feedback from actual users. Students are not expected to create accessibility solutions beyond applying established guidelines (e.g., Web Content Accessibility Guidelines [WCAG]).

practices.practice: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.
12. Design computing technologies that empower and inform users.

implementation_examples.description: Students design a grade calculator program by first composing a brief style guide that defines their color palette (ensuring high color contrast for accessibility), font choices, and standard icon placement for consistency. They construct a responsive user interface, plan for core functions to be easily discoverable across different devices, and secure accessibility features (e.g., text alternatives for images to account for diverse user needs).

Students develop a self-service kiosk interface for a specific public context (e.g., hospital check-in, public transit ticketing, library checkout system). They plan their interface by devising design decisions around items like usability, consistency, accessibility, error prevention, and user control, accounting for intended users such as individuals with limited mobility, visual impairments, limited English proficiency, or high-stress use conditions. Students construct the interface with features such as keyboard and touch alternatives, plain language, culturally neutral icons, and high-contrast visuals.

standards.statement: Use AI-assisted IDE tools or features to understand unfamiliar code and identify errors during debugging.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should use AI-assisted IDE tools or features for code comprehension and debugging tasks. This includes generating code summaries and documentation to understand unfamiliar or legacy code and using intelligent code completion, error detection, and refactoring suggestions during debugging. For example, students could use AI assistance to generate a summary explaining an unfamiliar function's purpose, inputs, and outputs before fixing a bug. Students should apply existing, commercially available, or open-source AI IDE features.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to manually configure or fine-tune the underlying machine learning models within the IDE (e.g., modifying the weights or architecture of the code-generation transformer model), integrate external non-IDE-based AI tools, or develop custom AI extensions for their IDE.

implementation_examples.description: Students implement a set of new requirements in an existing large, unfamiliar code base. To understand the existing structure, they implement the AI-assisted features in their IDE. They use the AI assistant to instantly generate docstrings or code summaries for several key functions, drastically reducing the time needed for code comprehension. While coding new features or modifying reported bugs, they use the AI's intelligent code completion and predictive error flagging to write correct syntax faster, and they investigate AI recommendations for code refactoring to simplify unnecessarily complex sections, ultimately demonstrating an increase in productivity and code quality.

Students investigate and find errors in an existing, open-source, unfamiliar software project (e.g., simulation, game engine module, data-processing script) by using AI-assisted features built into their IDE. To build understanding, students use the AI assistant to produce plain-language explanations, summaries, or inline comments for key functions and files, helping them quickly interpret the program's purpose and structure. While locating and fixing bugs, students use AI-supported debugging features to identify errors and find potential solutions. Students illustrate how AI-assisted IDE tools supported code comprehension and debugging while still requiring human judgment to verify correctness and intent.

standards.statement: Design a test plan that exercises program functionality, including edge cases, error conditions, and varied user inputs.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should create thorough and systematic test cases from both human and AI-generated sources. The plan should include a variety of test case types, such as unit tests and integration tests. Tests should cover valid input, edge cases, error conditions, user inputs, and other scenarios based on software use cases. Students should apply test cases systematically to a software project involving multiple functions and data structures.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to implement automated testing frameworks or manage quality assurance processes for large systems, nor to perform adversarial security testing (e.g., penetration testing). They are also not expected to design, train, or modify any underlying machine learning models used to generate AI test case recommendations.

implementation_examples.description: Students design a comprehensive set of test cases for a web-based survey application that collects and stores user input. They create systematic tests (either manually, using AI-assistance, or both) to verify core functionality, including correct handling of valid inputs, boundary values, empty or missing inputs, and invalid formats. Students also design tests for error conditions to ensure that the application handles unexpected or problematic inputs appropriately. They make appropriate documentation for each test case with its purpose, expected outcome, and observed results, using this process to identify issues and refine the program's reliability.

Students design a comprehensive test plan for a command-line or desktop application that processes user-generated data (e.g., a grade calculator, budgeting tool, file-renaming utility). Students create systematic test cases (either manually, using AI assistance, or both) that verify core functionality, including correct handling of valid inputs and expected outputs, as well as edge cases (e.g., boundary values, empty or missing inputs, invalid data types). They also design tests for error conditions, such as unavailable files or incorrect command usage, to ensure that the program fails safely and provides clear feedback. Students develop documentation for each test case with its purpose, input values, expected results, and observed behavior.

standards.statement: Collaborate to develop software that reflects diverse perspectives.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should work in teams on a shared software project, with team members contributing to different components. They should use version control tools to manage workflows, including branching, reviewing code, resolving merge conflicts, and integrating work through pull requests. Teams should establish inclusive norms that actively incorporate diverse perspectives on code design, user experience, and ethical considerations, including respecting intellectual property through appropriate attribution, licensing, and responsible reuse of code and media. For example, students might develop a multi-module program using version control, where pull requests are reviewed not only for technical quality but also for usability and ethical implications, ensuring that insights drawn from varied areas of expertise (e.g., user communities, UI design, accessibility, data privacy) inform final decisions.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to administer version control servers, manage repository security policies, or integrate version control with continuous integration/continuous deployment pipelines.

practices.practice: 2. Respect others' rights and dignity when creating computing technologies.

implementation_examples.description: A student team programs a large-scale application (e.g., a simple social networking platform, a large data analysis tool). The team develops their project using Git. Each student is assigned a specific module or feature and creates a feature branch for their work and ensures that they are respecting intellectual property while building. When a feature is complete, the student initiates a pull request to merge their code into the main branch. The other team members collaborate by performing review of the code and providing constructive written feedback on the code style, efficiency, and adherence to design specifications. The Git system helps the team with overall collaboration, including documentation, clear communication, and a respectful approach to conflicting code changes.

A student team builds a large-scale application using a real-time coding tool that allows for multiple developers to edit the same codebase simultaneously for pair programming or collaborative debugging sessions within their IDE. The team uses software development best practices to determine team roles and expectations while programming and editing the code. Students are required to maintain high-quality comments, including respecting intellectual property, while adding to and providing feedback for code.

standards.statement: Apply associative and hierarchical data structures to solve computational problems.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should select and apply appropriate associative and hierarchical data structures including dictionaries (hash tables), trees, graphs, and heaps to solve computational problems. Students should use built-in or library implementations and their associated methods. Students should use dictionaries for efficient key-value lookups, trees for hierarchical data or ordered collections, graphs for modeling networks and relationships, and heaps for priority-based access. Students should explain relative efficiency trade-offs in practical terms (e.g., which operations are faster, which use less memory). For example, students might use a graph structure to find the shortest path in a navigation app, a dictionary to quickly look up student records by ID, or a tree to organize a file system hierarchy.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to implement these data structures or their operations from scratch. Students are not expected to use Big O notation to express time and space complexity.

implementation_examples.description: Students build a program to solve a pathfinding problem (e.g., finding the shortest route on a subway system map). Subway stations and lines are represented as a graph, where stations are nodes and lines are edges. The program then uses a graph traversal algorithm to find the most efficient route between two chosen stations.

Students build a program that manages emergency response coordination for a city. The system uses a graph to represent intersections and roads, enabling responders to analyze routes between locations; a dictionary (hash table) to store and quickly retrieve incident details by incident ID; a tree to organize response units within a command hierarchy (e.g., city → district → unit); and a heap (priority queue) to schedule incidents based on urgency and response time. Students use built-in or library implementations of these data structures.

standards.statement: Develop a prototype using diverse user personas and user journey maps to guide design decisions.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should create user personas and user journey maps to guide ideation and prototyping and justify design decisions. User personas represent different types of users and their characteristics, needs, and goals. User journey maps visualize how users interact with a product from initial contact through achieving their goals, highlighting pain points and opportunities for improvement. For example, when designing an educational app, students might create personas representing different user types (e.g., a student with a learning disability, a highly motivated student, a parent) and develop user journey maps for each persona to ensure the design addresses diverse needs.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to conduct market research to validate personas or produce fully functional applications.

practices.practice: 10. Understand and involve diverse users in design decisions.
12. Design computing technologies that empower and inform users.

implementation_examples.description: Students design a mobile app for a school club. Prior to building features, they first create three distinct user personas (e.g., a new, shy student, a busy senior who is already a member, a faculty advisor). For each persona, students create a user journey map that details their potential interactions with the app from initial discovery through all intended features. Based on the insights gained from these maps (e.g., the shy student's desire for a way to connect without face-to-face interaction), students then plan specific features and create a low-fidelity prototype to test their solutions. This iterative process, driven by the persona and journey map, ensures that the final design is more inclusive and user-focused.

Students develop a prototype for a community disaster preparedness website designed to support residents before and during emergencies. Students create multiple user personas (e.g., an elderly resident with limited technical experience, a parent coordinating family safety, a non-English-speaking community member seeking critical updates). For each persona, students create a user journey map that traces how the individual would learn about the site, access information, and take action during an emergency. Using insights from these journeys, students design and create prototypes of key interface features (e.g., simplified navigation, multilingual alerts, offline-accessible resources), making their design decisions based on the needs revealed by the personas and journey maps.

standards.statement: Develop a project in iterative cycles, documenting changes and the rationale for each cycle.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should develop a software project using an iterative process. This includes breaking the project into multiple distinct cycles of planning, implementation, testing, review, and documentation that continuously refine and build project features. Students should document each cycle with a clear record of changes made and the reasoning behind them (e.g., bug fix, new feature, response to user feedback). For example, in one cycle a student might build a basic user login system, in the next cycle add a user profile feature, and in a third cycle implement a search function.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to use formal, complex project management methodologies like Agile or Scrum and their specific ceremonies (e.g., daily stand-ups, sprint retrospectives).

implementation_examples.description: Students design a portfolio website. In the first iterative cycle, they build the basic structure, including an index page and an About Me section. They document this as "Cycle 1: Basic Site Structure," noting the files created and a brief rationale. In the second cycle, they add a gallery section for their projects, documenting the new features and explaining why they were added. In the third cycle, they configure a responsive design to ensure the site looks good on mobile devices, documenting this decision as a response to the need for mobile accessibility. This iterative process, with its focus on documented cycles, allows students to build the project in manageable chunks, reflect on their progress, and adapt to new requirements as they go.

Students develop a high school sports team management tool, such as a practice planner or player performance tracker, using clearly defined iterative development cycles. In the first cycle, students build a basic version that allows entry and display of player names and practice schedules, documenting the features completed and the rationale for their initial design choices. In later cycles, students incrementally add new features (e.g., tracking attendance, recording basic performance stats, improving the user interface) and document each change, along with the reason it was made (e.g., coach feedback, usability issues). This iterative process emphasizes building software in manageable stages while reflecting on how each cycle improves the project.

standards.statement: Modify an existing algorithm to improve efficiency, considering factors such as data structures and algorithmic paradigms.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should identify opportunities to improve efficiency in terms of time or space complexity in algorithms. This involves understanding how different data structures (e.g., arrays, dictionaries, trees) impact performance and selecting a more suitable one. Students should apply algorithmic paradigms (e.g., divide and conquer) to break a problem into smaller subproblems. Students should use this information to modify and optimize existing solutions, measuring performance. For example, a student might improve a linear search algorithm for a large, sorted dataset by using a more efficient data structure and applying binary search.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to invent new algorithmic paradigms.

implementation_examples.description: Students improve the efficiency of an existing program that uses a simple linear search to find a specific word in a large text file. They investigate the algorithm, noting that it has to check every single word in the worst-case scenario. They modify the program to improve its search time. They sort the list of words, perhaps by using a divide-and-conquer sorting algorithm (e.g., mergesort or quicksort) and then replace the linear search with a more efficient binary search algorithm. This demonstrates a concrete application of improving an algorithm's efficiency by changing the data structure (from an unsorted list to a sorted one) and applying a different algorithmic paradigm.

Students improve the efficiency of an existing program used to analyze player statistics for a high school sports season (e.g., finding the top scorer, locating a specific athlete's record in a large dataset). The initial version of the program uses an inefficient approach (e.g., repeatedly scanning a list of player records to answer each query). Students investigate the performance limitations of this approach and then modify the algorithm to improve efficiency by selecting more appropriate data structures or algorithmic strategies (e.g., organizing records in a dictionary for faster lookups, sorting data once and using a more efficient search method). Students connect how their modifications reduce the number of operations required with the revised approach being more efficient in practical terms.

standards.statement: Evaluate the user experience to improve usability.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should conduct usability evaluations on digital interfaces by observing user interactions, collecting qualitative and quantitative feedback, and documenting findings in a structured format. For example, students could create a user survey or think-aloud protocol to test a peer's program or a real-world app and compile a report outlining specific usability issues (e.g., confusing navigation, inaccessible features).
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to obtain research ethics approval, recruit participants from outside of their peer group, or use specialized usability testing tools (e.g., eye-tracking software). Students are not expected to perform statistical analysis beyond calculating basic descriptive statistics for survey questions (e.g., average ratings, distribution of responses to Likert-type items).

practices.practice: 10. Understand and involve diverse users in design decisions.

implementation_examples.description: Students participate in a peer review activity where they trade programs with a peer and, as evaluators, conduct a usability test. This involves asking the evaluator to perform a specific task while the programmer observes for difficulties and takes notes. The evaluator verifies their experience through a detailed report that documents the program's strengths and weaknesses and suggests specific, actionable improvements based on their observations.

Students administer a usability evaluation of a school-related digital tool (e.g., an online bell schedule viewer, a lunch ordering system, an athletics sign-up page. Students evaluate a small group of users completing specific tasks (e.g., finding an event time, submitting a form), using methods such as think-aloud protocols, observation checklists, or short surveys to collect both qualitative and quantitative feedback. They validate points of confusion, errors, completion time, and user comments in a structured report and evaluate key usability issues. Based on their findings, students justify clear, actionable improvements that address navigation, clarity, accessibility, or feedback, demonstrating an evidence-based approach to evaluating user experience.

standards.statement: Create user-friendly, accessible, and responsively designed interfaces.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should create user interfaces for digital products that are usable, accessible, and responsive across different devices and screen sizes by applying UI design principles and tools. For example, students could develop a web application that adapts its layout and functionality to be effective on smartphones, tablets, and desktop computers, ensuring that elements are navigable and legible for users with different needs.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to create applications that function on every possible device and operating system or master responsive design frameworks.

practices.practice: 10. Understand and involve diverse users in design decisions.

implementation_examples.description: Students redesign a simple web page for a local nonprofit to be more user-friendly and responsive. They first use the existing site on different devices (e.g., a phone and a desktop) to investigate UI issues. They then propose and implement a new design that uses responsive principles to optimize the layout for each screen size. They also ensure the site includes accessibility features such as sufficient color contrast and proper alt text for images.

Students design and implement a user interface for a school or community service tool (e.g., a volunteer sign-up page, an event calendar, a tutoring request form) using UI design principles and digital design tools. Students create an interface that is easy to navigate, visually clear, and accessible, applying principles such as readable typography, sufficient color contrast, logical layout, and clear interactive elements. The interface must be responsive, adapting appropriately to different screen sizes (e.g., phones, tablets, desktops).

standards.statement: Use IDE tools to test and refine complex software projects.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should use IDE tools and features, including AI-assistive tools, to enhance the testing and refinement phases of a complex software project. This includes features for automated test generation (e.g., unit test boilerplate, test cases), identifying redundant or inefficient tests and receiving real-time suggestions for code optimization and performance improvements during the refinement phase. Students could write a new class, use an AI tool to generate a basic suite of unit tests for it, review and critique the generated tests for test coverage, and then accept the IDE's AI-driven recommendation to refactor a slow loop into a more performant structure.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to perform deep-dive performance profiling, interpret low-level hardware performance counters, or manually implement complex statistical analysis of test results derived from large-scale, enterprise-level performance testing tools. The "complex software project" should remain within the scope of advanced high school application development (e.g., multi-module, multifile application with external libraries).

implementation_examples.description: Students are working on a multifile project with a complex data processing module. After implementing a new feature, they use their AI-assisted IDE to automatically generate unit tests for their new code. They then critique the generated test cases, manually adding complex edge cases that the AI missed, thereby improving their overall test coverage. During the refinement phase, the IDE flags a section of code as having low performance. The student then applies the AI's suggested code optimization to reduce the computational complexity of the function, confirming the speed improvement through informal timing.

Students refine a large, multifile software project (e.g., a simulation, a data analysis tool, a game subsystem) using AI-assisted features within their IDE. After adding or modifying functionality, students use the IDE's AI tools to generate automated tests and review the suggested test cases for completeness, identifying missing edge cases or interaction scenarios. Students then extend the test suite to improve coverage and reliability. During refinement, students also use AI-assisted diagnostics to identify performance bottlenecks or code quality issues and apply suggested optimizations, validating improvements through testing or basic performance checks. The assignment emphasizes using AI tools as supports for testing and refinement while maintaining student judgment and responsibility for final decisions.

standards.statement: Debug complex software projects to identify, isolate, and fix errors.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should systematically apply formal debugging methodologies (e.g., divide and conquer, binary search, backtracking) to software projects involving multiple files, libraries, and external dependencies. This includes using advanced IDE debugger tools and features such as AI-assisted debuggers, setting conditional breakpoints, inspecting the call stack and watch window for complex data structures, and remote debugging. For example, students could debug a multi-module program with a subtle bug by reproducing the error, isolating the fault by tracing state changes across functions, and then implementing a fix. Students should focus on logical program errors.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to debug at the operating system level, such as analyzing assembly code, directly manipulating memory registers, or performing post-mortem memory dump analysis for errors in production operating systems or hardware drivers.

implementation_examples.description: Students debug a complex software project (e.g., a simple database management system, a multithreaded application, a program interacting with an external API) containing a known, non-obvious logical error. Using an IDE, students must first hypothesize where the bug is and then apply a systematic technique (e.g., binary search debugging) to efficiently isolate the faulty module. They then use the IDE's debugging features to pinpoint the exact line of code causing the error. Finally, they fix the error and verify the fix by running the full test suite.

Students debug a complex, multi-module software project (e.g., scheduling system, game engine component, data-processing pipeline) that contains a hidden logical or runtime error. Students begin by forming hypotheses about possible sources of the bug and apply a systematic debugging strategy (e.g., isolating components, using divide-and-conquer techniques) to narrow down the issue. Using IDE debugging tools, students set breakpoints, inspect variables, analyze the call stack, and trace program execution to identify the precise cause of the error. After implementing a fix, students verify correctness by rerunning tests or reproducing the original failure scenario, demonstrating a structured and disciplined approach to debugging.

standards.statement: Apply industry-standard software development processes to plan and deliver projects while prioritizing equity and justice.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should select and apply an industry-standard software development process (e.g., Agile Scrum, Kanban, Waterfall) to a medium- to large-scale project. Students should effectively use project-management tools to manage tasks, track progress, and communicate with team members. Students should demonstrate that equity and justice are non-negotiable priorities that override technical or budgetary pressures and articulate and justify project modifications based on ethical or societal impacts. For example, a student team could adjust a project timeline and scope to prioritize features that improve accessibility for users with disabilities or mitigate algorithmic bias, even if it delays the release or requires refactoring complex code. Students should engage in development projects of appropriate complexity for high school, with a focus on applying sound processes and prioritizing ethical considerations.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to manage the budget or financial resources of the project, use advanced proprietary or enterprise-level project management software, or manage external stakeholders beyond their classroom or school environment.

practices.practice: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.

implementation_examples.description: A student team develops a public-facing mobile application (e.g., a community resource locator). The team selects the Scrum development process, establishing roles, setting up a Kanban board on a digital tool, and defining features in a product backlog. Midway through a two-week sprint, the team realizes a crucial feature for low-literacy users requires a complex, time-consuming change to the user interface design. This feature was not initially scheduled but is identified as a critical equity and justice priority. The team halts existing work, documents the ethical justification for the change, reprioritizes the backlog, adjusts the project timeline, and redistributes tasks to ensure that the high-priority, equitable feature is delivered, demonstrating the principle of prioritizing societal impact over technical deadlines.

Students work in teams to plan and deliver a software project that addresses a real community need (e.g., a school transportation information tool, mutual-aid coordination platform, language-accessible event notification system) using an industry-standard development process (e.g., Scrum, Kanban). Teams define roles, create a project backlog, and plan iterative work cycles while explicitly identifying equity and justice considerations for their intended users. During development, teams are presented with a scenario in which a previously overlooked user group (e.g., users with disabilities, limited internet access, nondominant languages) requires a design or functionality change that affects the project plan. Students document the ethical reasoning behind reprioritizing work, adjust timelines and responsibilities, and reflect on how software development processes can be used to center equity and justice alongside technical goals.

standards.statement: Explain connections between CS concepts and practices and those from a non-CS discipline (X).
standards.boundary_includes: Students should identify and explain, at a conceptual level, how foundational computer science principles, such as data representation, algorithmic thinking, or abstraction, support understanding or problem-solving within a non-CS field (X) such as economics, linguistics, or art history. For example, students in a literature class could explain how word frequency analysis relies on data representation to convert text into numerical features and algorithmic processing to identify patterns across a large corpus, enabling insights about authorial style or thematic emphasis that would be difficult to detect through close reading alone.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to develop models that computationally solve advanced domain-specific problems.

math.standard: Understand that a function from one set (called the domain) to another set (called the range) assigns to each element of the domain exactly one element of the range. If f is a function and x is an element of its domain, then f(x) denotes the output of f corresponding to the input x. The graph of f is the graph of the equation y = f(x).
math.description: Students explain how a mathematical function like f(x) = 2x + 1 mirrors procedural abstraction in computer science. They identify that a function name serves as a shortcut for a set of operations, that inputs map to parameters, and that the output corresponds to a return value. Students articulate how this connection helps them understand both algebraic functions and CS procedures as reusable, named processes that transform inputs into outputs according to defined rules.

ela.standard: Analyze the impact of the author’s choices regarding how to develop and relate elements of a story or drama (e.g., where a story is set, how the action is ordered, how the characters are introduced and developed).
ela.description: Students explain how CS concepts such as sequence, iteration, and pattern recognition connect to analyzing narrative structure. They identify how a story's plot follows a defined sequence of events and how characters undergo repeated cycles of conflict and growth, mirroring the concept of iteration in computing. Students articulate how recognizing these structural patterns across multiple works reveals a shared logical framework underlying diverse narratives.

science.standard: Use the periodic table as a model to predict the relative properties of elements based on the patterns of electrons in the outermost energy level of atoms.
science.description: Students explain how the periodic table functions as an organized data structure, where each element's position encodes properties such as reactivity and atomic mass. They identify how CS concepts like abstraction (grouping elements by shared properties rather than by individual characteristics) and conditional logic (e.g., predicting an element's behavior based on its group and period) parallel the way data is structured and queried in computing. Students articulate how treating the table as a searchable database reveals patterns that connect chemistry to computational thinking.

social_studies.standard: Critique the usefulness of historical sources for a specific historical inquiry based on their maker, date, place of origin, intended audience, and purpose.
social_studies.description: Students explain how the CS concept of data cleaning connects to evaluating primary source documents in history. They identify parallels between filtering unreliable or inconsistent data in a dataset and identifying bias, gaps, and inconsistencies in historical archives. Students articulate how both processes require establishing criteria for what counts as reliable information and systematically applying those criteria before drawing conclusions.

standards.statement: Formulate a computational solution to a problem in a non-CS discipline (X) using computational thinking.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should identify a problem in another discipline (X) that can be addressed using computational thinking. They decompose the problem into subproblems, identify patterns or important variables (abstraction), and develop step-by-step procedures (algorithms) that describe a possible solution. For example, biology students studying population dynamics could model how a prey population changes over time by identifying key variables (e.g., birth rate, predation rate, available resources) and designing an algorithm that describes population changes across generations. Students should focus on documenting the design process using tools such as pseudocode or flowcharts.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to create, test, and refine a full computational solution.

math.standard: Explain why the x-coordinates of the points where the graphs of the equations y = f(x) and y = g(x) intersect are the solutions of the equation f(x) = g(x); find the solutions approximately, e.g., using technology to graph the functions, make tables of values, or find successive approximations. Include cases where f(x) and/or g(x) are linear, polynomial, rational, absolute value, exponential, and logarithmic functions.
math.description: Students formulate a computational approach to finding x-intercepts. They decompose the problem by identifying that repeatedly narrowing a search interval (the Bisection Method) can locate a zero. Students design the algorithm in pseudocode, specifying the inputs (function, interval, tolerance), the iterative logic (split the interval, check which half contains the zero), and the stopping condition. Students document how this approach transforms a difficult algebraic problem into a repeatable logical process.

ela.standard: Determine two or more themes or central ideas of a text and analyze their development over the course of the text, including how they interact and build on one another to produce a complex account; provide an objective summary of the text.
ela.description: Students formulate a computational approach to analyzing a novel's thematic structure. They decompose the problem by identifying theme-related keywords and designing a simple scoring rule (e.g., classifying words as positive or negative). Students use a flowchart to document how the algorithm would process each chapter, calculate tone scores, and produce a visualization of how the story's emotional arc shifts over time. Students explain how this approach could make literary analysis more systematic and evidence-based.

science.standard: Use mathematical and/or computational representations to support explanations of factors that affect carrying capacity of ecosystems at different scales.
science.description: Students formulate a computational approach to modeling predator-prey dynamics. They decompose the system into key variables (e.g., birth rate, predation rate, carrying capacity) and design a step-by-step algorithm using pseudocode or a flowchart that describes how populations change month by month through iteration. Students identify how a single change (e.g., a drought, an increase in predators) would propagate through their model and document the expected behavior of the system.

social_studies.standard: Integrate evidence from multiple relevant historical sources and interpretations into a reasoned argument about the past.
social_studies.description: Students formulate a computational approach to identifying patterns across historical primary sources. They decompose the problem by selecting a set of documents from a specific historical period and identifying key variables to track (e.g., frequency of specific terms, rhetorical patterns, references to particular events). Students design an algorithm in pseudocode that describes how a word frequency counter would process the documents and produce a summary of dominant ideas, documenting how this approach could support evidence-based historical arguments.

health.standard: Evaluate the effectiveness of health-related decisions.
health.description: Students formulate a computational approach to assessing wellness risks. They decompose complex health habits (e.g., sleep, diet, exercise) into measurable variables and design a decision-tree algorithm using a flowchart that maps combinations of inputs to risk levels. Students document how each decision branch reflects health guidelines and explain how the algorithm could be used to help individuals identify areas for improvement.

standards.statement: Analyze a computer science technology or approach used in a non-CS discipline (X).
standards.boundary_includes: Students should investigate a specific computer science technology or approach, detailing the foundational computing concepts involved, how it was developed, and its real-world impact on the chosen non-CS discipline. For example, students could analyze how machine learning algorithms are used in medical imaging to detect tumors, detailing the training process using labeled image datasets, the pattern recognition methods that identify abnormalities, and how this approach has improved diagnostic accuracy and speed.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to reproduce the innovation, implement it from scratch, or conduct comprehensive analyses of its societal, economic, or policy implications beyond describing its direct impact on the discipline

practices.practice: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.

math.standard: Represent data on two quantitative variables on a scatter plot, and describe how the variables are related.
math.description: Students analyze how algorithmic trading systems use algebraic concepts to make automated financial decisions. They investigate how these systems apply linear functions and trend lines to model price movements, how they use slope to measure the rate of change in stock prices, and how they evaluate inequalities to trigger buy or sell actions when prices cross defined thresholds. Students detail the foundational computing concepts involved (e.g., iteration, conditional execution, real-time data processing) and describe how the combination of algebraic modeling and automated decision-making has changed the speed and scale of financial markets.

ela.standard: Analyze and evaluate the effectiveness of the structure an author uses in his or her exposition or argument, including whether the structure makes points clear, convincing, and engaging.
ela.description: Students analyze how natural language processing (NLP) uses computational methods to identify patterns in text. They investigate how NLP algorithms apply pattern recognition to track features such as word frequency, sentence structure, and sentiment across large volumes of text and how these techniques have been used for tasks like authorship attribution and tone analysis. Students detail the foundational computing concepts involved (e.g., data representation, pattern recognition, algorithmic processing) and describe how NLP has expanded the tools available for literary scholarship.

science.standard: Design, evaluate, and refine a solution for reducing the impacts of human activities on the environment and biodiversity.
science.description: Students analyze how precision agriculture uses AI algorithms and sensor networks to optimize resource use on farms. They investigate how sensors collect real-time data on soil moisture, nutrient levels, and weather conditions and how algorithms process this data to make decisions about irrigation and fertilization. Students detail the foundational computing concepts involved (e.g., data collection, conditional logic, feedback loops) and describe how this approach has reduced water and chemical use in real-world farming operations.

social_studies.standard: Use geographic data to analyze variations in the spatial patterns of cultural and environmental characteristics at multiple scales.
social_studies.description: Students analyze how Geographic Information Systems (GIS) use computational methods to support urban planning decisions. They investigate how GIS technology uses abstraction to organize real-world geographic data into structured layers (e.g., population density, transit routes, green space distribution) and how query logic (e.g., identifying areas with high population but few parks) enables planners to target interventions. Students detail the foundational computing concepts involved and describe how GIS has been used to inform decisions about resource allocation and community development.

health.standard: Evaluate the validity, reliability, and accessibility of health information, products, services, and other resources.
health.description: Students analyze how wearable fitness trackers use a data pipeline to convert raw sensor measurements into actionable health information. They investigate how sensors collect physiological data (e.g., heart rate, step count), how iterative sampling processes monitor the body continuously, and how conditional logic determines when to trigger alerts or display progress. Students detail the foundational computing concepts involved (e.g., data collection, iteration, conditional logic, data visualization) and describe how wearable technology has influenced personal health monitoring.

arts.standard: Generate melodic, rhythmic, and harmonic ideas for a collection of compositions (representing a variety of forms and styles), improvisations in several different styles, and stylistically appropriate harmonizations for given melodies.
arts.description: Students analyze how algorithmic composition uses computational methods to generate music. They investigate how composers and programmers translate rules of harmony and rhythm into algorithmic instructions, how iteration is used to produce and evaluate musical variations, and how conditional logic governs decisions about melodic and harmonic structure. Students detail the foundational computing concepts involved (e.g., rule-based systems, iteration, conditional logic) and describe how algorithmic composition has expanded the tools and methods available to musicians.

standards.statement: Model relationships within a non-CS discipline using data, visualizations, and computational methods.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should select and apply computational methods (e.g., sorting and filtering, grouping and aggregating, calculating new variables) to structure, analyze, and visualize a real-world dataset from a non-CS discipline (X), revealing patterns and relationships within that discipline. For example, social science students could organize raw voting records into a structured dataset, calculate voter turnout by district, and create visualizations to reveal geographic patterns in political participation.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to develop novel computational methods or algorithms. Students are not expected to work with datasets that require memory or processing power beyond what is available on their personal devices.

math.standard: Fit a function to the data; use functions fitted to data to solve problems in the context of the data. Use given functions or choose a function suggested by the context. Emphasize linear, quadratic, and exponential models.
math.description: Students organize a real-world dataset (e.g., the relationship between height and shoe size, between study time and test scores) into a structured format and create scatter plots to visualize relationships between variables. They calculate new variables (e.g., differences from the mean, ratios) to explore the strength and direction of relationships and use grouping to compare patterns across subsets of the data. Students connect their visualizations to algebraic concepts by describing observed relationships in terms of positive or negative association and approximate rate of change.

ela.standard: Analyze how an author’s choices concerning how to structure a text, order events within it (e.g., parallel plots), and manipulate time (e.g., pacing, flashbacks) create such effects as mystery, tension, or surprise.
ela.description: Students organize the text of a novel or collection of works into a structured dataset by extracting word frequencies by chapter or section. They use sorting and filtering to identify the most common terms, grouping to compare vocabulary patterns across sections, and calculating new variables (e.g., the frequency of specific theme-related words per chapter relative to total word count). Students create visualizations that reveal how language patterns shift across the text, connecting observed trends to narrative structure (e.g., increased frequency of conflict-related words during rising action).

science.standard: Develop and use a model to illustrate the hierarchical organization of interacting systems that provide specific functions within multicellular organisms.
science.description: Students organize information about cell organelles into a structured dataset, with variables representing each organelle's function, location, inputs, and outputs. They use sorting and filtering to group organelles by function (e.g., energy production, protein synthesis, transport) and create visualizations that reveal how different organelles relate to each other within cellular processes. Students filter for specific organelles (e.g., those involved in energy production) and create a diagram showing how materials flow between them.

social_studies.standard: Analyze the reciprocal nature of how historical events and the spatial diffusion of ideas, technologies, and cultural practices have influenced migration patterns and the distribution of human population.
social_studies.description: Students organize raw historical data about migration events (e.g., dates, origins, destinations, number of people) into a structured dataset. They use sorting, filtering, and grouping to identify patterns (e.g., peak periods of movement, common routes, regional differences) and create visualizations (e.g., timelines, maps, bar charts) that reveal the scale, direction, and timing of historical migration. Students articulate how their computational methods reveal patterns in the data that would be difficult to identify from narrative sources alone.

health.standard: Evaluate practices, behaviors, and other factors supporting individual and collective health and well-being.
health.description: Students collect daily data on sleep duration and self-reported wellness indicators over several weeks and organize it into a structured dataset. They use sorting and filtering to identify patterns (e.g., wellness scores on days with more or fewer hours of sleep), grouping to compare weekday versus weekend patterns, and calculating new variables (e.g., average sleep over rolling three-day windows). Students create line graphs or other visualizations to reveal relationships between sleep habits and wellness outcomes.

arts.standard: Select, organize, and document personal musical ideas for arrangements, songs, and compositions within expanded forms that demonstrate tension and release, unity and variety, balance, and convey expressive intent.
arts.description: Students work with a structured representation of a musical piece (e.g., a spreadsheet derived from a MIDI file) where each note is a record with variables for pitch, duration, dynamics, and position. They use sorting and filtering to identify patterns (e.g., recurring motifs, pitch ranges by section), grouping to compare structural sections (e.g., verse vs. chorus), and calculating new variables (e.g., average note duration per section). Students create visualizations that reveal structural relationships within the composition and articulate how data representation connects to music theory concepts such as form, repetition, and contrast.

standards.statement: Assess how well an algorithm solves problems within a non-CS discipline (X) by evaluating its accuracy, efficiency, and relevance to the intended goal.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should evaluate and select appropriate metrics for assessing accuracy, efficiency, and relevance based on the algorithm being analyzed. Students should also explain trade-offs between accuracy and efficiency and justify the suitability of the algorithm in the context of the discipline (X). For example, students in a geography class could assess a routing algorithm used in a mapping application by evaluating whether it finds the shortest path accurately, how quickly it processes routes as the number of intersections increases, and whether it accounts for factors that matter in the local context (e.g., road closures, pedestrian-only zones, accessibility for wheelchair users).
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to formally derive algorithmic complexity using Big O notation.

practices.practice: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.

math.standard: Calculate and interpret the average rate of change of a function (presented symbolically or as a table) over a specified interval. Estimate the rate of change from a graph.
math.description: Students assess two algorithms (the rectangle method and the trapezoidal method) for estimating the area under a curve. They evaluate accuracy by comparing each method's estimate to a known answer, and they evaluate efficiency by counting how many iterations each method requires to reach a given level of precision. Students explain why the trapezoidal method converges faster for smooth curves and articulate how choosing the right algorithm for a given mathematical problem involves balancing computational effort against accuracy.

ela.standard: Cite strong and thorough textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text, including determining where the text leaves matters uncertain.
ela.description: Students assess an authorship attribution algorithm that uses pattern recognition to analyze word choices and sentence structures across a body of text. They evaluate accuracy by examining how often the algorithm correctly identifies a known author from a test set, efficiency by considering how the algorithm's performance changes as the volume of text increases, and relevance by assessing whether the features the algorithm analyzes (e.g., word frequency, sentence length) are meaningful indicators of authorial style. Students explain the trade-offs involved and discuss whether algorithmic analysis alone is sufficient for literary attribution.

science.standard: Evaluate a solution to a complex real-world problem based on prioritized criteria and trade-offs that account for a range of constraints, including cost, safety, reliability, and aesthetics, as well as possible social, cultural, and environmental impacts.
science.description: Students assess two algorithms used to predict how well a drug molecule binds to a protein target. They compare a faster algorithm that screens many candidate molecules but produces more false positives against a slower algorithm that is more accurate but processes fewer candidates in the same amount of time. Students evaluate accuracy (e.g., the rate of correct predictions) and efficiency (e.g., the number of molecules screened per hour) and explain the trade-offs researchers face when choosing between speed and precision in drug discovery.

social_studies.standard: Analyze how people use and challenge local, state, national, and international laws to address a variety of public issues.
social_studies.description: Students assess a predictive policing algorithm that uses historical crime data to forecast where crimes are likely to occur. They evaluate accuracy (e.g., whether predictions match actual crime locations), efficiency (e.g., how quickly the algorithm processes data across a city), and relevance (e.g., whether the algorithm accounts for factors that matter to the community, such as overpolicing of certain neighborhoods). Students explain how bias in historical data can undermine accuracy and discuss the trade-offs between computational efficiency and equitable outcomes.

health.standard: Examine how self-efficacy, perceived susceptibility, and perceived severity affect health behaviors.
health.description: Students assess a screening algorithm that flags individuals for further medical testing based on health indicators. They evaluate accuracy by examining the rates of false positives (flagging healthy individuals) and false negatives (missing individuals who are actually at risk) and efficiency by considering how many records the algorithm can process in a given time. Students explain the trade-offs between these metrics and discuss how the consequences of errors differ depending on the context of the screening (e.g., increasing sensitivity to catch more true cases also increases false positives, meaning that more healthy individuals will endure unnecessary further testing).

arts.standard: Develop and refine a determined range of creative and adaptive innovation abilities, such as design thinking, and risk taking, in addressing identified challenges and constraints within and through media arts productions.
arts.description: Students assess algorithms used in digital audio effects (e.g., reverb, pitch correction). They evaluate efficiency by measuring latency (the delay between input and processed output) and accuracy by comparing the fidelity of the processed audio to the intended result. Students explain the trade-offs between speed and quality (e.g., a low-latency algorithm is essential for live performance but may sacrifice audio fidelity, whereas a high-fidelity algorithm is preferable for studio recording where processing time is less constrained).
